items.title: Co-occurring pain-related functional limitation and tobacco/alcohol use is associated with unmet care in U.S. adults.
items.authors: Qeadan F, Faucher A, Thornquist R.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: Pain that limits daily functioning often co-occurs with tobacco and alcohol use, but population-level data on unmet treatment needs are limited.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We analyzed 2022 Medical Expenditure Panel Survey data for adults (n = 10,777). Pain-related functional limitation was defined as pain limiting normal work "moderately," "quite a bit," or "extremely", and substance use was defined as tobacco use "every day" or "some days" and/or alcohol use at least monthly. We created a four-level profile (neither, pain only, substance use only, both) and used survey-weighted logistic regression to examine associations with three measures of unmet care including two household-level cost-related measures (delayed medical care due to cost and inability to afford medical care) and one person-level measure (needing counseling or treatment but not getting it). Regression models used outcome-specific complete cases.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Overall, 42.6% of adults had neither pain nor substance use, 8.9% had pain only, 42.0% had substance use only, and 6.6% had both. Compared with neither, pain-only respondents had higher odds of reporting household-level delayed care due to cost (aOR [95% CI] = 1.99 [1.34, 2.95]) and inability to afford medical care (aOR [95% CI] = 2.52 [1.62, 3.93]); respondents with both pain and substance use also had elevated odds (aOR [95% CI] = 1.78 [1.22, 2.59] and aOR [95% CI] = 2.81 [1.80, 4.37], respectively). Substance use only was not associated with either household-level cost-related outcome but was associated with person-level unmet mental health treatment (aOR [95% CI] = 1.44 [1.19, 1.73]), as was the pain + substance use group (aOR [95% CI] = 1.65 [1.20, 2.26]). Adjusted pairwise contrasts showed that the co-occurrence group had higher odds than the tobacco/alcohol-use-only group for household-level delayed care (aOR [95% CI] = 1.86 [1.25, 2.76]) and inability to afford care (aOR [95% CI] = 3.26 [2.01, 5.28]), but did not differ significantly from the pain-only group for either outcome.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Pain-related functional limitation, with or without tobacco/alcohol use, was associated with household-level cost-related unmet care. Tobacco/alcohol-use-only and co-occurring profiles were associated with person-level unmet mental-health treatment. The co-occurring group did not have significantly higher adjusted odds of any outcome than the pain-only group. Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify temporality and evaluate strategies for improving access to pain and behavioral healthcare.

items.title: The lived experience of fathers navigating partners with postpartum depression: a phenomenological study.
items.authors: Ma H, Luk BHK, Ma Y, Chu TY, Wong JY.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a common mental disorder among women following childbirth. Fathers play a crucial role in supporting mothers and children during this period, yet limited research exists on the impact of maternal PPD on fathers in Hong Kong.

sections.heading: Aim
sections.text: This study aims to provide insights into the lived experience of fathers navigating partners with PPD in Hong Kong.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Using a purposive sampling technique, individual interviews were conducted with 23 fathers whose partners experienced PPD symptoms within 12 months after childbirth. Qualitative data were analyzed using Colaizzi's seven-stage descriptive phenomenological approach. Ethics approval was obtained from the Research Ethics Committee (REC) of the Hong Kong Metropolitan University prior to the study (Ref No. HE-RD/2023/2.16).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Five key themes emerged: (1) Empathic understanding of PPD: Fathers exhibited a nurturing and emotionally sensitive form of masculinity. (2) PPD as a shared journey: Navigating the challenges of PPD fostered mutual bonding and a strengthening of family relationships. (3) Unexpected Transition to a sole primary caregiver: Many fathers felt unprepared for the substantial parenting responsibilities. (4) Navigating emotional sacrifice: Fathers prioritized the well-being of their partners and children over their own. (5) Resilience through flexibility, joy, and social support: Despite the challenges, fathers derived strength from witnessing their children's growth and their social networks.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study highlighted the complex experiences of fathers navigating their partners' PPD in Hong Kong, emphasizing the need for targeted support to address the challenges they face and enhance the well-being of their families.

items.title: Research on the relationship between mental health and physical health of college students: a retrospective cohort study.
items.authors: Lin Z, Ding W, Su M.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: This study aims to examine the prospective associations between college students' baseline psychological symptoms and their subsequent physical fitness outcomes to provide a scientific basis and practical reference for the formulation of mental health education in colleges and universities and strategies for promoting their physical fitness.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective cohort study with longitudinal physical fitness follow-up selected 6,491 undergraduate graduates from six consecutive admission cohorts (2019-2024) at a comprehensive university as the research subjects. The Symptom Checklist-90 (SCL-90) was used to assess their psychological symptoms, and their physical fitness test scores were incorporated into the analysis. Correlation analysis, group comparisons, and linear mixed-effects models were employed to examine the associations between psychological symptoms and physical fitness test results.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: There were significant differences in the scores of obsessive-compulsive, depressive, anxious, and phobic factors on the SCL-90 between male and female college students, with female students scoring higher than male students, although all differences were small in magnitude (Cohen's d < 0.25). Students with higher first-year physical fitness test scores tended to have lower SCL-90 factor scores than those in the lower-score group did, but the differences were very small (ε² ≤ 0.001) and only paranoid ideation and additional items remained significant after Bonferroni correction. Weak negative correlations were observed between most psychological symptom factors and both physical fitness outcomes. After Bonferroni correction, six of the ten SCL-90 factors remained significantly negatively correlated with the comprehensive physical fitness GPA. Linear mixed-effects models showed that physical fitness test scores declined significantly across the four academic years (B = -0.888 per year, P < 0.001), whereas baseline psychological symptom severity was not significantly associated with either the level or the rate of change of fitness scores.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Baseline psychological symptoms showed weak and largely non-significant prospective associations with subsequent physical fitness outcomes; cross-sectional associations were more evident for the comprehensive physical fitness GPA than for first-year fitness scores, and baseline symptom severity was not significantly associated with the four-year fitness trajectory.

items.title: Altered Directed Connectivity Between the Posterior Limb of the Internal Capsule and Cortical Gray Matter in First-Episode Drug-Naive Schizophrenia.
items.authors: Ding Q, Xu L, He H, Gao B, Xia L.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Schizophrenia is increasingly conceptualized as a dysconnectivity disorder involving both gray-matter and white-matter systems. White-matter (WM) abnormalities have been identified early in the disease course, including in first-episode and never-medicated patients. Among these, the posterior limb of the internal capsule (PLIC) has shown structural and microstructural alterations associated with symptom severity. Resting-state functional studies have also implicated the insula, superior temporal gyrus, and superior frontal gyrus in early schizophrenia, supporting these regions as plausible targets for WM-GM directed connectivity analysis.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study investigated causal interactions between white-matter seed regions in PLIC and 48 cortical gray-matter regions in patients with first-episode drug-naive schizophrenia using resting-state functional MRI and Granger causality analysis. Group differences were evaluated with false discovery rate correction.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Four significant alterations in directed connectivity were identified after correction. Compared with healthy controls, patients showed reduced directed influence from the left PLIC to the insula, increased directed influence from the superior frontal gyrus to the bilateral PLIC, increased directed influence from the superior frontal gyrus to the right PLIC, and reduced directed influence from the bilateral PLIC to the anterior superior temporal gyrus. These findings indicate direction-specific reorganization of white-matter-gray-matter interactions in early schizophrenia, characterized by weakened PLIC output to salience- and temporal-related cortical regions and enhanced frontal input to the PLIC. In addition, the strength of superior frontal gyrus-to-PLIC connectivity was positively correlated with positive symptom severity.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: First-episode drug-naive schizophrenia is associated with abnormal directed functional coupling between the PLIC and specific cortical regions. The pattern of reduced PLIC efferent influence and increased frontal afferent drive suggests that early schizophrenia involves selective reorganization of white-matter-gray-matter causal interactions rather than nonspecific disconnection. Enhanced frontal-to-PLIC connectivity may be particularly relevant to psychotic symptom expression.

items.title: Bupleuri radix and Bupleurum -Containing Formulas for Depression: Ethnopharmacological Rationale, Active Material Basis, Gut-Liver-Brain Pharmacology, and Translational Perspectives.
items.authors: Cheng Y, Zhang ZQ, Song JY, Lin TC, Yi LT.

sections.text: Bupleuri radix (Chaihu) is used in traditional Chinese medicine for emotional and digestive complaints, usually within multi-herb preparations. This structured narrative review aims to critically synthesize depression-related evidence across Bupleurum -containing formulas, herb pairs, extracts/fractions, and isolated constituents, distinguish preparation-specific findings from mechanistic and clinical inference, and identify priorities for future studies. The literature is synthesized by intervention identity, experimental context, mechanistic validation, exposure, and safety. Most mechanistic evidence comes from rodent stress models and cell systems. Reported effects involve neuroendocrine signaling, neuroinflammation, synaptic markers, microbial metabolites, and hepatic metabolism; causal perturbation supports selected pathways in specific preparations and models. These findings cannot establish a unified gut-liver-brain mechanism or identify the contribution of Bupleuri radix within every formula. Human studies concern heterogeneous populations, including major depressive disorder and depressive symptoms accompanying medical illness. Some trials report symptom improvement, but small samples, variable preparations, incomplete blinding, and limited adverse-event reporting constrain clinical conclusions. Pharmacokinetic studies further show that chemical abundance does not establish target-relevant exposure, while experimental and observational safety signals warrant preparation-specific evaluation. The gut-liver-brain framework is therefore presented as a testable working model. Progress requires authenticated preparations, exposure-matched mechanistic experiments, and adequately powered clinical trials with prespecified outcomes and systematic safety assessment.

items.title: Immuno-Metabolic Depression: From Immune-Metabolic Dysregulation to Biomarker-Guided Precision Psychiatry.
items.authors: Godvarthi R, Pathak SS, Patel SS, Singh SA, Wankhade P, Warbhe R, Narwade S.

sections.text: Immuno-metabolic depression (IMD) describes the clustering of atypical energy-related symptoms, low-grade inflammation, and metabolic dysregulation within major depressive disorder. This structured narrative review evaluates its biological basis and potential utility for patient stratification and treatment selection. PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library were searched through July 2026 without a lower publication-date restriction. Clinical, genetic, multi-omics, and neuroimaging evidence links energy-related symptom profiles with inflammatory and metabolic abnormalities. Human observations and preclinical experiments implicate interacting immune, metabolic, endocrine, kynurenine, dopaminergic, and gut-brain pathways, although an IMD-specific causal sequence remains uncertain. C-reactive protein, symptom profiles, and metabolic indices may support research stratification; their ability to predict differential treatment benefit requires validation. Anti-inflammatory and dopaminergic studies report preliminary mechanistic or symptom-related findings in selected samples, while exercise has shown favorable effects on immunometabolic indices. The reviewed semaglutide trial did not demonstrate benefit for the primary executive-function outcome or depressive symptoms, despite favorable secondary findings for global cognition and weight. IMD therefore remains a research framework with potential clinical relevance. Standardized definitions, longitudinal studies, and adequately powered randomized trials are needed to establish whether biomarker-guided treatment selection improves depressive, functional, and cardiometabolic outcomes beyond standard care.

items.title: Anxiety, Somatic Symptoms, and Skin-Picking Behaviors in Gifted and Non-Gifted Youth.
items.authors: Jimenez-Perianes A, Reyes JJ, Egea-Romero P.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Studies on the emotional and behavioral functioning of intellectually gifted children and adolescents have reported mixed findings, and few have examined anxiety, somatic symptoms, and skin-picking behaviors together. This study compared these dimensions in gifted and non-gifted youth, examining their associations and exploring differences by sex and developmental stage. Methods: This cross-sectional study included 290 participants aged 6-17 years (47 gifted and 243 non-gifted). Intellectual giftedness was defined as a Full-Scale IQ ≥ 130 and creativity ≥ the 75th percentile. Anxiety was assessed using the Revised Children's Manifest Anxiety Scale (CMAS-R), somatic symptoms using the Children's Somatization Inventory (CSI-24), and skin-picking behaviors using three exploratory items. Group comparisons, factorial analyses, and correlations were conducted. Results: No significant group differences were found in somatic symptoms. Gifted participants showed higher skin-picking behavior scores, with a moderate effect size, and higher anxiety ranks, with a small effect size. Exploratory analyses identified interactions between giftedness and sex for anxiety and somatic symptoms, but no significant interactions between giftedness and developmental stage. Small positive associations were observed among the three variables. Conclusions: Differences associated with intellectual giftedness varied across the dimensions assessed and did not indicate generalized emotional vulnerability. The higher skin-picking scores should be interpreted cautiously given the exploratory, non-diagnostic nature of the measure and should not be considered evidence of excoriation disorder. These findings highlight the importance of assessing emotional, somatic, and behavioral manifestations separately and support further research using larger samples and validated instruments.

items.title: Modifiable Factors Associated with Adolescent Mental Health: Evidence from the Spartanburg County Youth Risk Behavior Survey.
items.authors: Hossain MB, Hampton M.

sections.text: Background: This study examined demographic, school, behavioral, social, and academic factors associated with adolescent mental health and assessed in an exploratory analysis whether the association between academic performance and persistent sadness differed by sex. Methods: We analyzed data from 1112 adolescents participating in the 2022 Spartanburg County Youth Risk Behavior Survey. Survey-weighted logistic regression models examined persistent sadness and suicide planning, and survey-weighted ordinal logistic regression examined poor mental health. Models adjusted for demographic characteristics, bullying, school connectedness, feeling unsafe at school, physical activity, sleep, screen time, caring-adult support, and academic performance. Results: Female and bullying exposure were associated with higher odds across all three mental health outcomes, whereas longer sleep duration and greater caring-adult support were associated with lower odds across all three outcomes. Greater school connectedness was associated with lower odds of suicide planning and poor mental health, but not significantly with persistent sadness. Feeling unsafe at school was associated with persistent sadness and suicide planning, while greater screen time was associated with persistent sadness and poorer mental health. Academic performance was not independently associated with the outcomes overall. However, its association with persistent sadness differed by sex ( p = 0.014). Higher academic performance was associated with lower odds of persistent sadness among female students, but not among male students. A sensitivity analysis combining sparse academic-grade categories showed a similar directional pattern, although the interaction did not reach statistical significance ( p = 0.060). Conclusions: These findings identify potentially modifiable factors across school, behavioral, and relational contexts and illustrate how locally administered Youth Risk Behavior Survey (YRBS) data can inform school- and community-based adolescent mental health prevention planning and future research, while recognizing the observational nature of the findings.

items.title: Creatine as a Neuroenergetic and Molecular Target in Depression: A Narrative Review of Mechanistic and Clinical Evidence.
items.authors: P Cunha M, Shayan Akhtar A, Ramos-Hryb AB.

sections.text: Major depressive disorder (MDD) is a leading cause of disability worldwide, and one-third to two-thirds of patients do not reach remission after successive monoaminergic treatments. Impaired brain bioenergetics, including mitochondrial dysfunction and altered brain high-energy phosphate levels, has been proposed to contribute to the anergic, cognitive, and fatigue-related symptoms of MDD. Through the creatine kinase-phosphocreatine (CK-PCr) system, creatine buffers ATP in time and space and supports the fluctuating energy demands of synaptic transmission and plasticity. In this narrative review, we summarize creatine metabolism and critically appraise the preclinical evidence implicating monoaminergic, purinergic, NMDA receptor and nitric oxide, PI3K/Akt/mTORC1, GSK-3β/Nrf2, and BDNF signaling, redox and neuroinflammatory control, and hippocampal neurogenesis in the antidepressant-like effects of creatine. We then review the human evidence, including phosphorus-31 magnetic resonance spectroscopy (31P-MRS) studies of brain high-energy phosphates and randomized trials of adjunctive creatine, and we discuss why the clinical findings remain inconsistent. Human evidence suggests that oral creatine could reach the brain and increase total creatine, yet clinical efficacy has not been established, and existing trials were not designed to test the bioenergetic mechanism. We therefore propose trials that select the dose by 31P-MRS target engagement and stratify patients by bioenergetic markers.

items.title: A shared core, distinct network organization: urban-rural variation in ADHD-aggression networks and simulated intervention profiles among Chinese college students.
items.authors: Jiang Z, Cheng B, Chen H, Li S, Zhou J.

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD)-related difficulties are associated with aggression, but the connections between specific features of the two domains remain poorly understood in young adults. It is also unclear whether this organization varies across socioecological backgrounds.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This cross-sectional study mapped ADHD-aggression networks among 3,572 Chinese college students with urban or rural backgrounds. Six ADHD-related difficulties assessed with the Adult ADHD Self-Report Scale Screener and four aggression components assessed with the Buss-Perry Aggression Questionnaire were modeled as network nodes. We examined network structure, expected influence (EI), bridge expected influence (BEI), computer-simulated intervention profiles, and associations with peer relationship difficulties.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Task-initiation difficulty and hostility emerged as prominent central and bridge nodes in both networks, identifying a shared interface between self-regulatory difficulty and aggression-related cognition. The urban and rural networks nevertheless differed in overall structure and global EI. Exploratory comparisons suggested larger estimated weights for selected ADHD-related connections, higher expected influence for overactivity, and higher bridge expected influence for forgetfulness in the urban network. The alleviating simulations identified a shared set of leading nodes, with task-initiation difficulty showing the largest mean projected reduction in network activity in both groups. Moderation analyses identified FDR-significant interactions with residential background for several self-regulatory difficulties, indicating stronger associations with peer difficulties in rural-background students.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: These findings reveal a shared self-regulation-hostility interface within the ADHD-aggression system while showing variation in network organization and interpersonal relevance across urban- and rural-background students.

items.title: Feasibility of a Chatbot-Based Intervention to Support Case Management for Patients at Risk of Suicide in the Emergency Department: A Pilot Study.
items.authors: Choi H, Hwang S, Jeon C, An J, Yoo J, Heo S, Kim T, Kim M, Cha W, Chang H.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Emergency departments (EDs) are critical for suicide prevention, yet high workloads often hinder consistent case management. This pilot study assessed the clinical feasibility, usability, and acceptability of CAREBot, a rule-based chatbot designed to support ED-based case management for patients at risk of suicide, among patients and social workers.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We employed an explanatory sequential mixed-methods design. Ten patients and three social workers used CAREBot and completed questionnaires assessing usability, perceived usefulness, and satisfaction. Patients' psychological status was repeatedly assessed using the PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SBQ-R. Semi-structured interviews with social workers explored integration challenges and workflow impacts.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Patients rated ease of use (3.9/5) and information clarity (4.4/5) favorably, whereas emotional comfort was rated lower (2.5/5). Over 4 weeks, 191 URL access events were recorded among the 10 patients (mean, 19.1 per patient). Individual PHQ-9, GAD-7, and SBQ-R score trajectories varied across participants, with both increases and decreases observed. Social workers rated CAREBot favorably for quickly understanding patients' risk level or condition (4.33/5) and ease of following the scenario flow (5.0/5). Qualitative findings suggested that CAREBot could support initial patient assessments through structured digital screening, although social workers raised concerns regarding risk-scoring accuracy and the management of multiple high-risk patients.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: CAREBot appears to be feasible and acceptable as an adjunct to ED-based suicide case management, although these preliminary findings require confirmation in larger controlled studies. A rule-based architecture was deliberately selected to provide predictable and controlled interactions in a high-risk environment. Future research should evaluate whether integrating large language models (LLMs) with rule-based safety mechanisms can improve conversational responsiveness and personalization while maintaining patient safety.

items.title: Gender Bias in the Diagnosis of Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Systematic Review.
items.authors: Perez-Beltran M, Alda Díez JÁ, Farrés MGI, Del Campo MD, Roldán-Merino J.

sections.text: Background: This review examines gender differences in the diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Sex-related differences in ADHD recognition may reflect both symptom presentation and diagnostic judgment. Methods: A systematic review was conducted, and two empirical studies were ultimately included, each directly examining gender differences in ADHD diagnostic decision-making. The final search update was conducted on 18 October 2026, covering publications through 10 October 2026. No additional eligible studies were identified. Findings were synthesized narratively, and risk of bias was examined using RoB 2. Results: Both experiments reported higher odds of an ADHD diagnosis for vignettes describing boys than for otherwise equivalent vignettes describing girls. Both diagnostic decision results raised some concerns in the risk-of-bias assessment. Neither experiment directly established delayed diagnosis in girls or diagnostic error rates in routine clinical care. Conclusions: The two included experiments suggest that sex-related cues can influence ADHD diagnostic judgments under standardized conditions. The small evidence base, methodological concerns, and use of fictional cases limit generalization to clinical practice. Further research should examine whether these effects persist in routine assessments.

items.title: Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation for Depression During Pregnancy: A Narrative Review of Efficacy, Safety, and Practical Considerations.
items.authors: Ferraris Kandel D, Cristancho P, Marino B, Koo MB.

sections.text: Depression during pregnancy can require treatment decisions that balance illness severity, patient preferences, and concern about fetal medication exposure. This structured narrative review examined the efficacy of transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) during pregnancy, its maternal, obstetric, neonatal, and offspring outcomes, and its practical administration. PubMed, ProQuest Medical Library, JAMA Network, Google Scholar, Embase, and PsycINFO were searched. Thirty reports described at least 98 pregnancies with confirmed antenatal TMS exposure: one sham-controlled trial, three open-label series, one embedded pregnant subgroup, and 25 case reports or series. In the trial, depression scores decreased more with active than sham TMS (treatment-by-time p = 0.003), but response and remission differences were not statistically significant. Uncontrolled reports often described symptom improvement or maintenance without recurrence. Maternal adverse events were generally mild when reported; no maternal seizure was described during antenatal treatment, although ascertainment was uneven. The trial reported three late-preterm births among 11 active-arm participants and none among 11 sham participants. Longer-term comparative developmental follow-up was limited to one cohort. TMS appears feasible and may provide symptomatic benefit, but the literature does not establish comparative efficacy, definitive pregnancy safety, or a preferred protocol. Current evidence supports individualized consideration with coordinated obstetric and psychiatric care, alongside controlled studies and prospective surveillance.

items.title: Participant characteristics and health- and work-related outcomes associated with persistent musculoskeletal pain and common comorbidities: A cross-sectional study of UK biobank data.
items.authors: Liaghat B, Nicholl BI, Øverås CK, Skou ST, Ferreira P, Hanlon P, Folkestad L, Mair FS, Hartvigsen J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Persistent musculoskeletal (MSK) pain is prevalent and often co-occurs with other chronic conditions, which complicates clinical management.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: To examine the interaction between persistent MSK pain and common comorbidities for a range of participant characteristics and health- and work-related outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional analysis of UK Biobank data. Persistent MSK pain was defined as self-reported pain lasting >3 months. We identified seven prevalent comorbidities spanning multiple body systems (asthma, headache, cancer, cardiovascular diseases, type 2 diabetes mellitus, mental health conditions, and thyroid disease). Interaction effects between persistent MSK pain and comorbidities were assessed across participant characteristics (socioeconomic deprivation, BMI, physical activity, alcohol use, smoking, sleep problems) and health- and work-related outcomes (GP mental health visits, work status, pain medication use).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of the full cohort (N=498,531) (mean age 56.5 (SD 8.1)), females comprised 54%, and 38% reported persistent MSK pain. Among people with persistent MSK pain, 33.1% had no comorbidities, while 66.9% had ≥1. Interaction effects were generally small and varied by outcomes but were consistent across comorbidities. When pooled over all other comorbidities, average interaction estimates were statistically greater than expected for socioeconomic deprivation (OR 1.09, 95% CI 1.07; 1.12), BMI (OR 1.08, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.09), and physical inactivity (OR 1.05, 95% CI 1.00; 1.10), and statistically lower than expected for alcohol consumption (OR 0.91, 95% CI 0.89; 0.93).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Having both persistent MSK pain and one of seven prevalent comorbidities was associated with lifestyle and social characteristics, but generally not with health- and work-related outcomes.

items.title: A Perspective on Adjunctive/Combination Therapy in Major Depressive Disorder: What Have We Learned from Studies of Atypical Antipsychotics?
items.authors: Gao K, Oruc EB, Koparal B.

sections.text: Background and Objectives: To examine studies of atypical antipsychotics in the treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD), identify unmet needs in adjunctive therapy or combination therapy with antidepressant(s) in MDD, and discuss future directions in this area. Materials and Methods: The PubMed database was used to search for studies addressing definitions of treatment response in MDD and pivotal studies of adjunctive or combination therapy with atypical antipsychotics to an antidepressant in the treatment of MDD. The study designs and primary outcomes were extracted from original publications. The differences in study designs and reporting were narratively analyzed. Relevant systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis were also examined. Results: Eight atypical antipsychotics were studied in the treatment of MDD as an adjunctive therapy to an antidepressant or as a combination therapy with an antidepressant. Six of them were sponsored by pharmaceutical companies with an indication for MDD. Olanzapine and fluoxetine combination (OFC) was approved for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lumateperone, and quetiapine-XR were approved as an adjunctive therapy to an antidepressant for patients with MDD with "inadequate response". The study designs, especially inclusion and exclusion criteria and methodology to determine treatment response, were diverse. The study reporting in publications was inconsistent, and systematic reviews and meta-analyses commonly lumped all studies with different designs together for reporting and analyses. Conclusions: Standardized study designs and consistent reporting of clinical trials in adjunctive/combination therapy for MDD are urgent needs. Collaborations among regulatory agencies, pharmaceutical companies, and academics are essential to establish standard study designs for each indication. Journals and publishers should require detailed and unified reporting methods of clinical trials, especially for phase III trials, for indirect comparisons among the studies with systematic reviews and network meta-analyses.

abstract.text: Background and Objectives: To examine studies of atypical antipsychotics in the treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD), identify unmet needs in adjunctive therapy or combination therapy with antidepressant(s) in MDD, and discuss future directions in this area. Materials and Methods: The PubMed database was used to search for studies addressing definitions of treatment response in MDD and pivotal studies of adjunctive or combination therapy with atypical antipsychotics to an antidepressant in the treatment of MDD. The study designs and primary outcomes were extracted from original publications. The differences in study designs and reporting were narratively analyzed. Relevant systematic reviews with or without meta-analysis were also examined. Results: Eight atypical antipsychotics were studied in the treatment of MDD as an adjunctive therapy to an antidepressant or as a combination therapy with an antidepressant. Six of them were sponsored by pharmaceutical companies with an indication for MDD. Olanzapine and fluoxetine combination (OFC) was approved for treatment-resistant depression (TRD), and aripiprazole, brexpiprazole, cariprazine, lumateperone, and quetiapine-XR were approved as an adjunctive therapy to an antidepressant for patients with MDD with "inadequate response". The study designs, especially inclusion and exclusion criteria and methodology to determine treatment response, were diverse. The study reporting in publications was inconsistent, and systematic reviews and meta-analyses commonly lumped all studies with different designs together for reporting and analyses. Conclusions: Standardized study designs and consistent reporting of clinical trials in adjunctive/combination therapy for MDD are urgent needs. Collaborations among regulatory agencies, pharmaceutical companies, and academics are essential to establish standard study designs for each indication. Journals and publishers should require detailed and unified reporting methods of clinical trials, especially for phase III trials, for indirect comparisons among the studies with systematic reviews and network meta-analyses.

items.title: Development and Preliminary Psychometric Evaluation of the Preoperative Aesthetic Psychiatric Screening Scale (PASS-10).
items.authors: Roncea MG, Văsieșiu AM, Sălcudean A.

sections.text: Background and Objectives: Psychological vulnerability, body image dissatisfaction, anxiety, and depressive symptoms may substantially influence expectations, decision-making, and postoperative satisfaction among individuals seeking cosmetic surgery. Psychological screening is increasingly recommended during the preoperative assessment, brief and clinically applicable instruments specifically designed for cosmetic surgery candidates remain limited. This pilot study aimed to develop and perform a preliminary psychometric evaluation of the Preoperative Aesthetic Psychiatric Screening Scale (PASS-10). Materials and Methods: A cross-sectional pilot study was conducted among 142 adults considering cosmetic surgery procedures in Romania. Participants completed an anonymous online questionnaire including sociodemographic items, the newly developed PASS-10 questionnaire, and the Patient Health Questionnaire-4 (PHQ-4). Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha, McDonald's omega, and corrected item-total correlations. Exploratory factor analysis using principal axis factoring with Promax oblique rotation was performed to examine the factorial structure. Convergent validity was assessed using Spearman's rank correlation coefficient between PASS-10 and PHQ-4 total scores. Floor and ceiling effects and exploratory group differences according to sex were also examined. Results: The PASS-10 demonstrated good internal consistency (Cronbach's α = 0.854). Corrected item-total correlations ranged from 0.323 to 0.677. The Kaiser-Meyer-Olkin measure was 0.844, and Bartlett's test of sphericity was statistically significant (χ^2 = 506.733, p < 0.001), supporting the suitability of the data for factor analysis. Exploratory factor analysis using Promax rotation suggested a preliminary correlated two-factor solution explaining 55.97% of the total variance. The proposed two-factor structure remains exploratory and requires further validation in a larger, independent sample. No floor or ceiling effects were observed. PASS-10 total scores showed a moderate positive correlation with PHQ-4 scores (Spearman's ρ = 0.562, p < 0.001), providing preliminary evidence of an association with general anxiety and depressive symptoms. Male participants demonstrated significantly higher PASS-10 scores than female participants ( p = 0.003). Conclusions: The PASS-10 demonstrated promising preliminary psychometric properties, including good internal consistency and an exploratory two-factor structure. The association with PHQ-4 scores provides initial evidence of a relationship with general psychological distress. Further validation in larger, independent samples is required to confirm the factorial structure and establish the reliability and validity of the questionnaire.

items.title: Components and behavior change techniques applied in psychosocial interventions for substance use disorder treatment in Africa: A mixed-methods systematic review.
items.authors: Kiburi SK, Kuria S, Gitau C, Mbithi A, Jaguga F.

sections.text: Psychosocial interventions are effective treatments for substance use disorders (SUDs), but the components and behaviour change techniques (BCTs) used in these interventions in African setting have not been systematically reviewed. This review aimed to summarize the components, BCTs and effectiveness of psychosocial interventions in SUD treatment across Africa. This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines [PROSPERO registration CRD42024542926]. A search was conducted in five databases namely: PubMed/MEDLINE, The Cochrane Library, Web of Science, CINAHL and Academic Search Complete. BCT coding was done using BCT Taxonomy version 1. A narrative synthesis is provided for quantitative data and thematic analysis done for the qualitative findings. The search yielded 4168 articles of which 121 studies met the inclusion criteria, including 27 reporting qualitative data. Majority of the studies were conducted among adults, the commonest interventions were brief intervention, motivational interviewing and cognitive behaviour therapy. The findings showed effectiveness of psychosocial interventions in improving substance use and other outcomes such as mental and physical health symptoms although with mixed findings. Most studies reported at least one BCT application with a range of 1-14 BCTs per intervention. Categories with the most used BCTs were: goals and planning, feedback and monitoring, social support, and shaping knowledge and natural consequences while the least used were: associations, scheduled consequences, self-belief and identity. Qualitative data was summarized in four themes: perceived benefits; satisfaction and acceptability of intervention; perceived challenges/barriers; and recommendation for future interventions. Whilst, the heterogeneity of study designs, sample sizes, and outcome measures limited comparability across the studies, the findings in this review demonstrate the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions for SUDs treatment in Africa. Description of BCTs used provides an understanding of interventions' active ingredients and highlights opportunities for intervention improvement.

items.title: Deferasirox, an Oral Iron Chelator, Confers Antidepressant and Procognitive Effects in a Rat Model of Depression: Hippocampal Ferroptosis, Synaptopathy, and Neurodegeneration.
items.authors: Aboul-Fotouh S, Habib MZ, Elnahas EM, Aboul-Ela YM, Abdel-Latif GA, Abbas SS, Elshaffei IM, El Magdoub HM, Sadek DR, Eid DM, Elsyade RH, Mohamed SMY, Elshaer MMAR, Mahmoud Y, Khedr LH.

sections.text: Background: Disrupted iron homeostasis is increasingly perceived as a key driver of major depressive disorder pathogenesis; hence, targeting ferroptotic cascades may reveal novel therapeutic targets. This study evaluated the neuroprotective potential of the oral iron chelator deferasirox (DEF) against chronic unpredictable mild stress (CUMS)-induced depressive-like behaviors and cognitive deficits in Wistar rats. Methods: We specifically explored whether DEF could provide neuroprotection by targeting ferroptotic and oxidative stress pathways. Male Wistar rats were exposed to a 6-week CUMS protocol and treated with DEF (10, 20, or 40 mg/kg). Results: CUMS-exposed rats exhibited significant anhedonia, behavioral despair, and impaired spatial and recognition memory. Further analyses revealed a reduction in colonic and choroid plexus occludin, reflecting compromised structural integrity of both the intestinal and blood-CSF barriers, accompanied by enhanced hippocampal iron accumulation with increased Acyl-CoA synthetase long-chain family member 4 (ACSL4), Acyl-CoA synthetase family member 2 (ACSF2), and citrate synthase expression, alongside exaggerated oxidative stress and deficient neuroprotective mediators, specifically BDNF and synaptophysin, and increased neurofibrillary tangle (NFT) deposition, collectively exacerbating neurodegenerative pathology. DEF treatment ameliorated most of these effects, significantly reducing iron deposition, attenuating ferroptosis-related signaling, reducing oxidative stress, diminishing the ongoing neurodegeneration, and replenishing the depleted pool of BDNF and synaptophysin, which was accompanied by a reduction in depressive-like symptoms and improved cognitive functions. Conclusions: These findings support a link between ferroptosis-related signaling and depression-like phenotypes, reinforcing the concept of a metal-driven component in depression pathophysiology and offering a mechanistic rationale for further exploring targeting ferroptotic pathways and central iron regulation as potential targeted strategies in depression management.

items.title: Brain Drug Delivery for Major Depressive Disorder and Treatment-Resistant Depression: From Brain Exposure to Clinical Translation.
items.authors: Li Y, Li J, Zhao Z, Tang Y, Li Z, Wang C, Zhang T, Luo A, Hao Z.

sections.text: The treatment of major depressive disorder (MDD) and treatment-resistant depression (TRD) remains challenging because of delayed treatment onset, tolerability concerns, and the need for long-term management. Intranasal administration, molecular optimization, nanocarriers, blood-brain barrier (BBB)-targeted transport, and controlled drug release offer different approaches to improving antidepressant delivery. However, increased drug concentrations in the brain do not necessarily lead to better pharmacological effects; their value depends on whether the drug reaches its site of action and engages the relevant target. This review discusses the mechanisms, brain exposure, pharmacodynamic evidence, and clinical translation of different delivery strategies. Particular attention is given to the interpretive limitations of pharmacokinetic metrics and to the differences in evidence linking carrier distribution, functional cargo delivery, and antidepressant efficacy. Current clinical evidence is concentrated mainly on drugs that have entered clinical use, such as esketamine, whereas most novel targeted carriers and engineered extracellular vesicles remain at the preclinical stage. Their development requires identification of the specific drug-development bottleneck that each delivery system is intended to address, followed by validation of the relationships among effective brain exposure, pharmacological activity, safety, and formulation quality. An evaluation framework matched to the delivery mechanism may help determine whether delivery advantages observed experimentally can translate into meaningful therapeutic benefits.

Can Physical Exercise Buffer the Association Between Academic Stress and Depressive Symptoms Among Adolescents? Evidence from the 2020 China Family Panel Studies.
items.authors: Du Z, Zhao B, Zhu W, Zhai F, Yang G.

sections.text: Academic stress has been consistently associated with depressive symptoms among adolescents. Understanding whether physical exercise can buffer its negative effects is important for promoting adolescent mental health. Using data from the 2020 China Family Panel Studies, this study examined an unweighted analytical sample of 2789 school-attending adolescents aged 16-18 years. Hierarchical linear regression and a series of psychometric, diagnostic, and sensitivity analyses were employed to investigate the association between academic stress and depressive symptoms, the moderating role of exercise frequency, and gender differences in this association. Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) and SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) analyses were also conducted as exploratory complementary analyses. After adjusting for demographic covariates, academic stress was significantly and positively associated with depressive symptoms (B = 0.542, 95% CI [0.444, 0.640], β = 0.200, p < 0.001), whereas exercise frequency was significantly and negatively associated with depressive symptoms (B = -0.138, 95% CI [-0.195, -0.081], β = -0.089, p < 0.001), with the main-effects model explaining 5.9% of the variance (R^2 = 0.059). The interaction between academic stress and exercise frequency was significantly negative (B = -0.060, 95% CI [-0.113, -0.007], β = -0.041, p = 0.026, full model R^2 = 0.061), indicating that higher exercise frequency was associated with a weaker positive relationship between academic stress and depressive symptoms. However, the interaction explained only an additional 0.2% of the variance (Δ R^2 = 0.002), suggesting a modest buffering association that remained consistent across weighted, cluster-robust, Tobit, negative binomial, and multiple-imputation sensitivity models. An exploratory, non-preregistered three-way interaction model (R^2 = 0.063, Δ R^2 = 0.002, B = -0.080, 95% CI [-0.158, -0.002], p = 0.046) suggested gender differences in this moderating pattern, with a statistically significant conditional buffering association observed among male adolescents (B = -0.102, 95% CI [-0.178, -0.026], p = 0.009) but not among female adolescents (B = -0.022, 95% CI [-0.095, 0.051], p = 0.552). In the exploratory machine learning analyses, continuous XGBoost regression explained no additional out-of-sample variance beyond linear regression (R^2 = 0.061 vs. 0.060), and TreeSHAP interaction values confirmed a small interaction magnitude. Overall, these findings are consistent with the stress-buffering framework in the context of adolescent academic stress and describe associations in this cross-sectional Chinese sample; however, the interaction added little explanatory variance, and the cross-sectional observational design precludes causal inference.

items.title: Competing Factor Models and Subscale Reliability of the Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) in Mexican Undergraduate Cohorts.
items.authors: Cano-Ramírez H, Gutiérrez-Bravo MR, Hoffman KL.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-Revised (OCI-R) is a self-report measure of obsessive-compulsive symptoms that is widely used because of its validity in non-clinical samples. However, competing factor structures of the Spanish version of the OCI-R in Latin American undergraduate populations (particularly in Mexico) and measurement invariance across cohorts and gender remain unexamined.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This descriptive, serial cross-sectional study included three cohorts. Using non-probability convenience sampling, we recruited 798 undergraduate students from a Mexican university in 2023 (T1), 2024 (T2), and 2026 (T3). We compared one-factor, six-factor, and second-order models using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and assessed measurement invariance across cohorts and gender. Additionally, we estimated the reliability of the total and subscale scores with McDonald's ω and Cronbach's α, and calculated descriptive percentile scores.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The six-factor model showed acceptable fit by χ^2(120) = 815.67, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.947, TLI = 0.932, RMSEA = 0.085, 90% CI [0.080, 0.091], SRMR = 0.054 (ΔCFI = 0.079; ΔRMSEA = -0.042). The second-order model fit the data as the correlated six-factor model, χ^2(129) = 838.31, CFI = 0.946, TLI = 0.936, RMSEA = 0.083, 90% CI [0.078, 0.088], SRMR = 0.058. But the one-factor model did not fit well, χ^2(135) = 1871.55, p < 0.001, CFI = 0.868, TLI = 0.850, RMSEA = 0.127, 90% CI [0.122, 0.132], and SRMR = 0.083. Scalar invariance was supported across cohort (ΔCFI = -0.009) and gender (ΔCFI = -0.006). Internal consistency was high for the total score (α = 0.91; ω = 0.95) and ranged from 0.70 to 0.86 (ω) across subscales.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The Spanish OCI-R showed structural validity, measurement invariance, and reliable total scores in Mexican university students.

items.title: Eating Psychopathology and Alcohol Use in Food and Alcohol Disturbance Among Adolescents: A Person-Centred and Dimensional Analysis.
items.authors: Meneguzzo P, Suprani F, Paribello P, Deiana V, Milia P, Sanna L, Manchia M, Pes A, Carpiniello B, Pinna F.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Food and alcohol disturbance (FAD) comprises compensatory eating and weight-control behaviours occurring in relation to alcohol consumption. We examined whether eating-disorder psychopathology contributes to heterogeneity in adolescent FAD beyond alcohol-use severity alone.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Latent profile analysis was conducted in 2478 Italian high-school students using six Eating Disorder Inventory-3 dimensions and Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test (AUDIT) scores. Profiles were compared on FAD assessed with the Compensatory Eating and Behaviors in Response to Alcohol Consumption Scale (CEBRACS). Complementary dimensional analyses in a smaller subgroup (n = 1665) examined the independent and interactive associations of alcohol-use severity and eating-disorder risk with FAD.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Four profiles emerged: Eating Psychopathology (22.0%), Low-risk (17.1%), Alcohol-risk (33.5%), and High Psychopathology (27.4%). The Alcohol-risk and High Psychopathology profiles had similar mean AUDIT scores (6.15 vs. 6.21), but the latter showed significantly greater FAD. Eating-disorder risk explained additional variance beyond alcohol-use severity (ΔR^2 = 0.027), while the AUDIT × eating-disorder risk interaction accounted for a further ΔR^2 = 0.022 (B = 0.048, 95% CI [0.012, 0.084], p = 0.008). The association between alcohol-use severity and FAD strengthened as eating-disorder risk increased.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: Alcohol involvement was the primary correlate of FAD, while eating-disorder psychopathology provided additional explanatory information. These findings support considering both dimensions when assessing FAD, although the clinical utility of multidimensional screening remains to be established.

items.title: Financial Vulnerability Among Swedish Young Adults with Self-Reported ADHD: A Secondary Analysis of Cross-Sectional Survey Data.
items.authors: Samuelsson E, Levinsson H.

sections.text: The increasing prevalence of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) in Western countries highlights the need to better understand its impact on everyday functioning, including financial outcomes. This study examines financial vulnerability among Swedish young adults with self-reported ADHD diagnosis. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted among young adults ( N = 2057). Group differences were examined between individuals with self-reported ADHD diagnosis ( n = 149) and those without a psychiatric diagnosis ( n = 1380). Logistic regression analyses assessed associations between ADHD diagnosis, financial health variables (financial strain, financial self-control, and financial literacy), and indicators of financial vulnerability, controlling for age and gender. Individuals with self-reported ADHD exhibited significantly poorer outcomes across all financial health variables compared to controls. In the multivariable analyses, an ADHD diagnosis was significantly associated with two of the three indicators of financial vulnerability, with higher odds of taking out consumer loans without understanding the terms (OR = 2.4) and having informal debt to friends or relatives (OR = 1.8). ADHD was not significantly associated with outstanding consumer loan debt for more than 18 months (OR = 1.5). Young adults with ADHD may therefore be at increased risk of financial vulnerability, potentially reflecting a combination of financial, psychological, and behavioural factors. These findings may inform the development and future evaluation of financial education and support initiatives for young adults with ADHD.

items.title: Reframing Music Performance Anxiety: A Qualitative Case Study of a Mental Skills Intervention in Higher Education.
items.authors: Urhan G, Cornett V.

sections.text: Music performance anxiety (MPA) is a common psychological challenge experienced by university music students. It may negatively affect their well-being, self-confidence, academic engagement, and performance participation. Despite the importance of promoting student mental health in higher education, educational interventions addressing MPA remain limited. This study explored music students' experiences of a nine-week mental skills seminar designed to support the management of MPA. An exploratory qualitative case study was conducted with 17 students enrolled in music degree programmes at Ankara Music and Fine Arts University in Türkiye. Data were collected through individual semi-structured interviews conducted throughout the semester and focus group interviews held after the completion of the seminar, and were analysed using inductive thematic analysis. Participants reported improved self-awareness, greater ability to manage anxiety symptoms, increased confidence in performance preparation, enhanced psychological resilience, and more adaptive coping strategies. Breathing exercises, mental imagery, mindfulness practices, and peer sharing were identified as the most beneficial components of the intervention. These findings suggest that mental skills training may serve as a practical approach to supporting student well-being while helping music students manage performance anxiety. The results underscore the value of integrating mental skills training into higher education music curricula.

items.title: Risk and Frequency of Lifetime Suicide Attempts in Bipolar Disorder: Impact of Cloninger's Temperament and Character and Clinicodemographic Mediators.
items.authors: Foteinopoulos P, Prentakis A, Antoniou A, Constantinidi I, Stasinopoulou O, Efstathiou V, Rizos E, Ferentinos PP.

sections.text: Association of Cloninger's temperament and character with risk of lifetime suicide attempts in bipolar disorder (BD) has been investigated in few, often methodologically flawed studies, with inconsistent results. This study re-queried this association, also examining frequency of lifetime attempt(s), not previously investigated, and potential mediatory pathways. We recruited 178 euthymic patients with BD (111 BD-I, 67 BD-II). Temperament and Character Inventory (TCI-140) was administered. The effects of TCI dimensions on risk and frequency of attempts were investigated in logistic and negative binomial models, respectively. Mediation analyses were performed with 'CMAverse 0.1.0' R package within a counterfactual framework. A higher risk of attempted suicide was associated with higher harm avoidance (HA) and lower self- directedness (SD), while higher novelty seeking and self-transcendence were associated with a higher attempt frequency. No effect survived Bonferroni adjustment. Mediation analyses identified significant indirect effects of HA and SD on risk of attempts via BD-II subtype; indirect effects of other clinicodemographic characteristics were non-significant. Our study identified personality correlates of risk and frequency of lifetime attempts in BD and BD subtype as a potential mediator. These findings encourage research on the efficacy of psychopharmacological and psychotherapeutic interventions modifying temperament and character in the management of BD-associated suicidality.

items.title: The Role of Roommate Relationships Between Psychological Resilience and Chinese Freshmen's Depressive and Anxious Symptoms: A Three-Wave Longitudinal Study.
items.authors: Kong Y, Zhang K, Jiang Z.

sections.text: The transition to university life increases the susceptibility of freshmen to depression and social anxiety, especially facing new challenges of establishing new interpersonal relationships. Psychological resilience serves as a critical protective factor against these mental health challenges. Using three-wave data from 785 Chinese freshmen (52.1% female; M _age = 18.46), this longitudinal study revealed a relational pathway unique to female college freshmen: Psychological resilience contributed to female freshmen's roommate relationship quality, which further alleviated their depressive and anxious symptoms. In contrast, no significant direct or indirect pathways were observed among male freshmen. These findings underscore the dormitory microsystem as a crucial context for female students' emotional adaptation and suggest the need for gender-tailored interventions, such as resilience-building programs for female students and alternative support mechanisms for men.

items.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Approach for Predicting Depressive and Anxiety Symptoms After Treatment in Patients with Drug-Resistant Epilepsy.
items.authors: Xu Z, Zhao X, Wang H, Chen Y, Guo Y, Yao L.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Psychiatric comorbidities, particularly anxiety and depression, significantly impair quality of life and psychosocial functioning in patients with drug-resistant epilepsy (DRE). This study aimed to develop and evaluate interpretable machine learning (ML) models to predict post-treatment depressive and anxiety symptoms using exclusively pre-treatment baseline data.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Baseline demographic, clinical, and psychological data from a cohort of DRE patients were analyzed. Eight ML algorithms were trained and evaluated using repeated nested cross-validation to predict post-treatment depressive and anxiety symptoms as separate outcomes. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), Brier score, precision, recall, and F1-score. SHAP (SHapley Additive Explanations) analysis was performed for the Random Forest models to identify the key predictors for each outcome.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Five of the eight trained models achieved a mean AUC ≥ 0.80 for depressive symptoms, and seven for anxiety symptoms. Random Forest achieved the highest mean AUC for both depressive symptoms (0.838 ± 0.008) and anxiety symptoms (0.862 ± 0.011). SHAP analysis identified that baseline mood severity, treatment modality, and seizure-related variables as the primary predictors across both models.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The findings indicate that post-treatment depressive and anxiety symptoms in DRE patients can be predicted before treatment using routine baseline data, highlighting the potential of baseline clinical information for early risk stratification in this high-risk population.

items.title: Peripheral Inflammatory Indices in Major Depressive Disorder: Clinical Associations and Explainable Machine Learning.
items.authors: Ünal Demir F, Tasci B, Aydin S, Kocasaraç YM, Güneysu İ, Eser B, Yılmaz G, Özsoy F, Akpinar Aslan E.

sections.text: Background: The clinical relevance of routinely available peripheral inflammatory indices in major depressive disorder (MDD) remains uncertain, particularly regarding recent suicide attempts, depressive symptom severity, and their discriminative performance. This study investigated these associations using conventional statistical analyses and explainable machine learning. Methods: This retrospective, single-center study included 86 patients with MDD and 80 healthy controls. Six blood-derived inflammatory indices were examined for between-group differences and associations with recent suicide attempts and depressive symptom severity. Individual-marker discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic analysis, while three ensemble machine-learning models were evaluated using nested cross-validation and compared with MHR alone. Explainable artificial intelligence methods were applied to interpret model predictions. Results: Patients with MDD showed higher MHR, NHR, SIRI, and AISI values than controls. Recent suicide attempts were associated with higher SII, SIRI, and AISI, and these associations persisted after adjustment for age and sex; lower LHR was observed only in the unadjusted comparison and was not significant after adjustment. No inflammatory index was significantly associated with depressive symptom severity. MHR demonstrated the strongest individual discrimination. Machine-learning models showed modest discriminative performance without clear improvement over MHR alone, and feature-importance analyses consistently highlighted MHR. Conclusions: Here we show that peripheral inflammatory indices exhibit distinct observational associations with MDD and recent suicidal behavior. However, their diagnostic and predictive clinical utility remains unestablished and requires prospective, adequately controlled, independently validated studies.

items.title: A real diagnosis or just a Western trend? Navigating adult ADHD diagnosis and treatment in Saudi Arabia.
items.authors: Alhajji RAA, Alqahtani MMJ.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Little is known about how Saudi adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) recognize their symptoms, seek help, and navigate treatment. This study explored the experiences of Saudi individuals diagnosed with ADHD in adulthood.

sections.heading: Method
sections.text: Semi-structured virtual interviews were conducted with participants ( n = 17) diagnosed with ADHD during adulthood. The data were analyzed using a thematic analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Six themes, with 17 subthemes, were developed from participants' experiences: living with undiagnosed ADHD, recognizing ADHD and navigating pathways to diagnosis, emotional responses following diagnosis, sociocultural barriers and catalysts in the diagnostic pathway, navigating ADHD treatment, and adjustment to living with ADHD.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: In Saudi Arabia, an adult ADHD diagnosis intersects with family cultural norms and social skepticism, including perceptions of adult ADHD as an imported, fashionable "Western trend." These perceptions, together with family influence and stigma, may shape decisions regarding ADHD treatment.

items.title: Influence of harm-avoidance traits on anxiety: coping style as a mediator and CK1 gene polymorphism as a moderator.
items.authors: Ma H, Bu C, Liu N, Li M, Zhang Z, Cong Z.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: The mechanisms linking personality and anxiety remain incompletely understood. Thus, it is necessary to investigate the potential psychological and biological mechanisms. The present study examined the mediation effect of coping styles and moderation effect of the casein kinase 1 epsilon (CSNK1E; traditionally abbreviated CK1) gene polymorphism in this relationship.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The CK1 gene rs135745C/G polymorphism was genotyped in 556 healthy Chinese adults, and the personality traits, anxiety levels, and coping styles were assessed using the Tridimensional Personality Questionnaire, State-Trait Anxiety Inventory, and Simplified Coping Style Questionnaire, respectively.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: State and trait anxiety were positively related to the harm avoidance (HA) trait (both p < 0.01). Positive coping mediated the association between HA and its four subscales and both state and trait anxiety (all p < 0.01), and passive coping mediated the association between HA1, HA2, and HA4 and both state and trait anxiety (all p < 0.01). The rs135745 polymorphism moderated the association of HA with state ( p  = 0.008) and trait anxiety ( p  = 0.001). Simple slope analyses showed that the direction of the HA-anxiety association differed between genotype groups: it was negative in the small CC subgroup (n=8) (state: β = -1.3788, p  = 0.0485; trait: β = -1.7363, p  = 0.0105) and positive in G allele carriers (state: β = 0.4751, p  < 0.001; trait: β = 0.5186, p  < 0.001).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The present study demonstrates that Coping styles play a mediating role between HA and both state and trait anxiety in healthy Chinese adults, and provides preliminary evidence that the CK1 gene polymorphism may moderate this pathway, suggesting a potential gene-behavior interaction in the development of anxiety; the CC-specific pattern requires validation in larger cohorts.

items.title: Dissemination of Motivational Interviewing-Based Brief Intervention for Substance Use Disorders to HIV Service Organizations: A Cluster-Randomized Adaptive Dissemination Experiment Testing Facilitation as a Dissemination Strategy.
items.authors: Garner BR, Gotham HJ, Solinger E, Brinker J, Tueller SJ, Patel SV, Bradshaw M, Philbrick S, Mungo J, Donohoe T, Freese TE, Rutkowski BA, Roosa MR, Speck KJ, Knudsen HK.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Strategies that improve integration of evidence-based substance use disorder (SUD) innovations within HIV service organizations (HSOs) are needed. Building on research supporting the effectiveness of facilitation to improve HSOs' implementation of a motivational interviewing-based brief intervention (MIBI) for SUDs, this dissemination research sought to test the effectiveness of brief exploration facilitation to improve organization-level MIBI adoption/preparation (primary outcome) and exploration (secondary outcome) after an initial distributing educational materials strategy.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: HSOs that did not transition to adoption/preparation within one week of the initial distributing educational materials strategy were randomized to either (a) continue in the distributing educational materials condition or (b) receive exploration facilitation. Outcomes were assessed four months post-dissemination. The primary dissemination outcome was organizational-level adoption/preparation, defined as 1+ HSO staff downloading the manual and/or enrolling in online asynchronous training. The secondary dissemination outcome was organization-level exploration of the intervention (i.e., 1+ HSO staff opened the dissemination email).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: At the end of week 1 after the initial distributing educational materials strategy, 327 (46.7%) of 700 HSOs had transitioned to exploration and an additional 15 HSOs (2.1%) had transitioned to adoption/preparation. After randomization, no additional HSOs achieved adoption as a function of being in either study condition. Of 341 HSOs randomized to exploration facilitation, only 11 HSOs (3.2%) received the single facilitation session delivered by our team of facilitators.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: The project's initial distributing educational materials dissemination strategy led to minimal MIBI adoption by HSOs. Despite several phone attempts per HSO, the project's facilitators were generally unsuccessful in engaging HSOs and unable to deliver the exploration facilitation strategy; thus, the exploration facilitation strategy was not effective. Future research should consider testing alternative dissemination strategies, such as incentivization, which has demonstrated effectiveness as an implementation strategy.

items.title: Schizophrenia Burden in India Compared with the Global Population: Trends in Disease Burden, Demographic Drivers, and Future Projections Based on the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023
items.authors: Patel N, Kataria L, Patel A, Singh A, Gohil P, Jain A.

items.title: Dopamine Transporter Deficiency and Altered Glucose Homeostasis: Insights from DAT-Heterozygous Rats and Public Transcriptomic Data Analysis.
items.authors: Kanov EV, Fomicheva AA, Fesenko ZS, Sylko PA, Gainetdinov RR, Volnova AB, Vaganova AN.

sections.text: Dopamine regulates pleiotropic physiological processes, and its multifunctional nature is hypothesized to underlie the comorbidity between systemic disorders. For instance, neurodevelopmental conditions, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), are frequently accompanied by metabolic diseases that cannot be explained solely by lifestyle factors. We performed a secondary analysis of dopaminergic gene co-expression networks using large (N > 20) public RNA-seq datasets from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) repository to explore the potential links between the islet dopaminergic system and secretory activity. Additionally, pancreatic islet hormone levels and carbohydrate metabolism parameters were evaluated in an animal model of dopamine system dysfunction: heterozygous dopamine transporter gene knockout (DAT-Het) rats. No significant differences were observed in baseline serum glucose, insulin, glucagon, or somatostatin levels between DAT-Het rats and wild-type (WT) littermates. However, during a glucose tolerance test, DAT-Het rats exhibited a slight but significant decrease in glycated hemoglobin (HbA1c) serum levels and relative glucose levels 15 min after a glucose load. These findings indicate more active tissue glucose uptake in DAT-Het rats, potentially linking dopamine system dysfunction to both a neurodevelopmental phenotype and metabolic susceptibility. However, the precise role of pancreatic islets in this identified shift in glucose tolerance warrants further investigation.

items.title: Instability and Overinterpretation of Predictive Performance in a Small Multimodal Clinical Dataset: A Methodological Case Study of Adult ADHD Versus Other Psychiatric Disorders.
items.authors: Kolev M, Naskinova I, Lazarova M, Kalinov H, Klisurov V.

sections.text: Small public multimodal datasets invite overstated claims that wearable signals classify attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). The HYPERAKTIV dataset served as a methodological case study: 103 adult psychiatric outpatients, 51 with ADHD and 52 clinical controls, with actigraphy, heart-rate recordings, and cognitive testing. The task was differential classification, not screening. Background/Objectives: The objective is to quantify how far the reported performance depends on the evaluation protocol. Methods: The methods evaluated four nested feature blocks on 63 complete cases with one fixed model and one estimand: the mean out-of-fold area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) over 20 fold assignments. Each block was compared with a permutation null from the identical protocol. Results: The results are that the fold assignment alone moved a single block's AUROC by up to 0.235, and no block exceeded its null. The heart-rate-variability increment was -0.039 (percentile interval -0.153 to 0.155), inconclusive under every interval method. A bootstrap holding the fitted models fixed suggested a bounded null, and DeLong's test made the cognitive increment significant; resampling the whole pipeline confirmed neither. On datasets with the heart-rate-variability block permuted, these two tests rejected in 18.3% and 14.7% of those datasets at a 5% level. The pre-scored ADHD Confidence Index alone reached an AUROC of 0.743, descriptively above every fitted model. abstract.text: Small public multimodal datasets invite overstated claims that wearable signals classify attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). items.title: GLP-1-Based Therapies in Eating Disorder Recovery.
items.authors: Cunanan ALP, Zito K, Cho Y, Oliver R, Onyemailu V, Munn-Chernoff MA.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1)-based therapies, initially developed for glycemic control and now widely used for weight management, affect appetite, satiety, gastrointestinal function, and body weight in ways that may support or complicate eating disorder (ED) recovery. This review examines emerging evidence on GLP-1-based therapy use across ED presentations and considers implications for recovery-oriented care. Methods: We conducted a narrative synthesis of peer-reviewed research, review articles, and relevant clinical guidance addressing GLP-1-based therapy mechanisms, ED psychopathology and treatment, and recovery-related clinical and psychosocial considerations. Results: Evidence is most developed for binge-eating disorder (BED), but remains preliminary and inconsistent. Some observational findings suggest reductions in binge-eating symptoms, whereas a placebo-controlled trial found greater weight loss without a significant between-group difference in binge-eating episodes. Evidence for bulimia nervosa, anorexia nervosa, atypical anorexia nervosa, and other specified feeding or eating disorder presentations is sparse. For restrictive and purging presentations, appetite suppression, early satiety, delayed gastric emptying, and gastrointestinal adverse effects may reinforce restriction, complicate symptom monitoring, or interfere with nutritional rehabilitation. Conclusions: GLP-1-based therapies are not established treatments for ED psychopathology, and changes in weight, metabolic health, or selected symptoms should not be equated with multidimensional ED recovery. When these medications are prescribed for appropriate medical indications or investigated as adjunctive treatments, ED screening, informed consent, multidisciplinary monitoring, and assessment of psychological, nutritional, behavioral, and functional outcomes are warranted.

items.title: The NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 disrupts auditory-guided behavior through sex-dependent response channels in an operant oddball task.
items.authors: Lao-Rodríguez AB, Cacciato-Salcedo S, Liceran L, Mansilla M, Malmierca MS.

sections.text: Schizophrenia involves marked deficits in sensory-guided behavior, yet the behavioral consequences of N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) receptor hypofunction for auditory decision-making, and whether they differ by sex, remain unclear. We trained female and male rats on an operant auditory oddball task requiring responses to rare deviant tones (go context) while withholding responses to frequent standard tones (no-go context) across three inter-stimulus intervals (ISIs), and tested performance after a single dose of the NMDA receptor antagonist MK-801 using signal detection theory. We subcutaneously injected MK-801 (0.1 mg/kg; 0.075 mg/ml) to generate the drug-induced group, and saline solution 0.9% to produce the control group, across female and male rats. MK-801 reduced discrimination sensitivity, but through sex-dependent response channels. In females, the deficit was carried mainly by reduced correct detections of deviant tones, alongside a more conservative response criterion. In males, the sensitivity loss was weaker and ISI-dependent but was accompanied by increased false alarms to standard tones and faster false-alarm responses, indicating diminished response withholding. These effects were most pronounced at the longer ISIs and were expressed as immediate post-injection shifts rather than progressive session-by-session drift. We quantified all effects with linear mixed-effects models and Holm-corrected planned contrasts. Together, these findings show that acute administration of the NMDA receptor blockade disrupts auditory-guided behavior through dissociable, sex-specific response channels, providing a behavioral framework relevant to abnormalities associated with schizophrenia.
