items.title: A Study on Configurational Profiles of Vulnerability Conditions for Frequency-Based Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Severity Among University Students.
items.authors: Wang X, Zhou L, Sun Z, Xu X, Zhou J, Wang P.

sections.text: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) constitutes a significant public health issue among university students. Existing research commonly compares individuals with and without a history of NSSI; however, few studies have explored how multidimensional vulnerability conditions co-occur in relation to NSSI severity among individuals who have already engaged in NSSI. This study adopts a configurational approach to examine how eight antecedent conditions-family environmental risks (FERs), school environmental risks (SERs), vulnerable personality traits (VPTs), traumatic experiences (TEs), emotional symptoms (ESs), hazardous behaviors (HBs), negative life events (NLEs), and social support (SS)-co-occur in association with NSSI severity among university students with prior NSSI experiences, with the aim of generating hypotheses for future screening research. In total, 776 Chinese university students (61.3% female; Mage = 19.50, SD = 1.29) reporting at least one NSSI episode in the past year were recruited. Questionnaire data were collected using the Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Scale, Negative Life Events Scale, Social Support Scale, and a self-developed scale measuring distal vulnerability conditions of NSSI. A fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) was adopted to explore how eight antecedent conditions relate to the frequency-based NSSI composite score in this sample. One stable configuration is associated with high NSSI severity. When four prominent conditions-school environmental risks (SERs), traumatic experiences (TEs), emotional symptoms (ESs), and hazardous behaviors (HBs)-co-occur, accompanied by elevated negative life events (NLEs) and limited social support (SS), university students are more likely to exhibit high NSSI severity. Three equifinal configurations are identified for non-high NSSI severity. The first is characterized by low levels of traumatic experiences (TEs), emotional symptoms (ESs), and hazardous behaviors (HBs), together with few negative life events (NLEs), and is associated with non-high NSSI severity regardless of external social support (SS). The second and third are characterized by the co-occurrence of high social support (SS) alongside attenuated risk conditions. The configurations associated with high NSSI severity are not simply mirror images of those for non-high NSSI severity. Emotional symptoms (ESs) function as a core distinguishing condition between the two outcomes. Social support (SS) exhibits heterogeneous co-occurrence patterns rather than uniform associations with NSSI severity.

items.title: Agency, Not Attendance: Involuntary Boarding School Enrolment, Adult Separation Anxiety and Parenting Attitudes-A Cross-Sectional Study from Türkiye.
items.authors: Sarıkavak T, Elkin N.

sections.text: Objective: This study examines associations between adolescent boarding-school experiences and adult separation anxiety and parenting attitudes. Bridging sociological and psychiatric perspectives, we examined whether adult separation anxiety statistically accounts for the association between boarding-school experiences and parenting attitudes, and whether psychological resilience moderates this pathway. Methods: A cross-sectional online survey recruited 173 adults, including 117 participants with a boarding-school history recruited via snowball sampling across 42 institutions to maximize institutional heterogeneity and 56 participants in a non-boarding comparison group. Parenting attitudes were assessed exclusively in participants with children (n = 132). Analyses included covariate-adjusted ANCOVAs, hierarchical regressions, and bootstrap-based simple mediation (jAMM) to evaluate indirect pathways. Results: Boarding-school attendance alone did not determine maladaptive outcomes. Among participants with complete mediation-model data (n = 86), not being consulted about boarding attendance was associated with higher adult separation anxiety (β = 0.289, p = 0.005), and separation anxiety was associated with more protective parenting (β = 0.229, p = 0.035); the estimated indirect association was small (β = 0.066) and not robust across bootstrap procedures. The hypothesised moderating role of resilience was tested and not supported (a-path p = 0.990, b-path p = 0.345). In exploratory bivariate analyses, longer boarding duration was modestly associated with more over-tolerant parenting (r = 0.22, q = 0.047 after false-discovery-rate correction). In hierarchical regressions, boarding-school level accounted for additional variance in protective, authoritarian and over-tolerant parenting (ΔR^2 = 0.07-0.11, all p ≤ 0.006) but not in democratic parenting, which was predicted instead by the Perception-of-Self dimension of resilience (β = 0.46, p < 0.001). Higher educational attainment was likewise associated with more democratic parenting in covariate-adjusted comparisons (F(1, 128) = 8.91, p = 0.003, η^2p = 0.065). Conclusions: Perceived participation in boarding-school decisions and features of boarding exposure may be relevant to adult separation anxiety and parenting attitudes. These associations require testing in prospective, probability-sampled designs.

items.title: Applying the Transcreation Framework to Design the Recovery Coach Doula Role and Delivery Model to Support Individuals with Substance Use Disorder in the Perinatal Period.
items.authors: Thumm EB, Westmoreland B, Creel LM, Phillips EG, Lopez S, Anderson JL.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Treating perinatal substance use disorder is a public health priority. Social support is associated with better substance use and perinatal outcomes. Doula care and recovery coaching from peers who are in recovery themselves are two evidence-based interventions designed to provide social support. The aim was to braid doula care and peer recovery coaching into a novel healthcare personnel role and develop a delivery model for implementation in community settings.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A team led by community members from the recovery and birth justice communities and perinatal clinicians, with a policy analysts, and an implementation scientist applied the Transcreation Framework guided by extant literature, theory, formative research, and existing community infrastructure in weekly or biweekly sessions over three years.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The team identified a strong evidentiary foundation for Recovery Coach Doula care and supportive community infrastructure. Through theory analysis and formative research, the team identified 15 core functions of the Recovery Coach Doula role and developed a delivery model. The core functions were intentionally designed to be adaptable to allow Recovery Coach Doulas to meet the needs of their clients. To deliver Recovery Coach Doula care in community settings, the team created a hub and spoke model delivery program to accommodate varying healthcare models and center the needs of the Recovery Coach Doulas, as well as the clients. The transcreation process provided structure required for rigorous co-design over an extended period time with iteration.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Systematic application of the Transcreation Framework with community laid the foundation for implementation of Recovery Coach Doula care. Next steps include rigorously testing the effectiveness of Recovery Coach Doula care and developing implementation strategies and outcomes.

items.title: Association of Direct and Indirect Discrimination, Activities of Daily Living, and Social Support with Depressive Symptoms in Adults with Disabilities.
items.authors: Choi H, Bae SM.

sections.text: Depression is a prevalent mental health issue among individuals with disabilities and is frequently accompanied by discriminatory experiences and challenges in daily living. Despite its significance, the differential associations of direct and indirect discrimination with depression remain underexplored. This study aimed to investigate the independent associations of direct and indirect discrimination experiences with depression, while accounting for activities of daily living and social support. This was a cross-sectional secondary analysis of data collected in South Korea in 2023 through the 18th wave of the Korea Welfare Panel Study, specifically a supplementary survey on individuals with disabilities. A total of 1345 adults with disabilities were included, of whom 81.5% were aged 60 years or older and 51.7% were women. Descriptive statistics and correlation analyses were conducted using SPSS 23.0, and hierarchical regression analysis was employed to examine the associations of key variables with depression. Indirect discrimination was significantly associated with higher levels of depression ( β = 0.134, p < 0.001) after accounting for sociodemographic characteristics, ADL, IADL, and social support, whereas direct discrimination was not significantly associated with depression. Higher IADL functioning ( β = -0.245, p < 0.001) and greater social support ( β = -0.133, p < 0.001) were associated with lower levels of depression, while ADL was not significantly associated with depression. These findings indicate that indirect discrimination, but not direct discrimination, was independently associated with depression among adults with disabilities. They highlight the importance of addressing structural and environmental forms of discrimination and strengthening psychosocial resources for adults with disabilities.

items.title: Associations Between Sleep Quality and Anxiety Among Undergraduate Engineering Students: A Longitudinal Panel Study.
items.authors: Cao X, Liu X.

sections.text: Sleep is important to university students' mental health, but longitudinal evidence on associations between sleep and anxiety is limited among engineering undergraduates. Using a three-wave balanced panel of 281 engineering undergraduates (W1-W3) at a Chinese university, this study examined longitudinal associations among sleep quality, sleep duration, and anxiety symptoms using a cross-lagged panel model, complemented by individual fixed-effects and adjacent-wave change-score analyses. Anxiety symptoms and sleep-quality problems were descriptively higher at W2 and W3 than at W1, while average sleep duration changed little. Poorer sleep quality at W2 was significantly associated with higher anxiety at W3, and higher anxiety at W2 was significantly associated with poorer sleep quality at W3. Average paths in both directions across the two adjacent-wave intervals were significant; interval-specific reciprocal prospective associations were statistically detectable only from W2 to W3. Independent cross-lagged associations between sleep duration and anxiety were generally weak. Complementary analyses showed significant contemporaneous within-person associations and synchronous changes between deteriorating sleep quality and increasing anxiety. These findings advance the understanding of the relationship between sleep quality and anxiety and may inform further research on sleep support and anxiety risk identification in demanding educational contexts.

items.title: Defense Styles Beyond Internalizing and Externalizing Symptoms: A Cross-Sectional Study of Early Adolescent Outpatients.
items.authors: Koullourou I, Sharp C, Hyphantis T, Mantas C, Karagiannopoulou E, Salum GA, Kotsis K.

sections.text: Borderline personality traits (BPTs) in adolescence overlap substantially with internalizing and externalizing symptoms, while defensive functioning is also closely intertwined with these symptom dimensions. Beyond this interdependence, defense styles may provide complementary information about aspects of psychological functioning relevant to BPTs. This secondary cross-sectional analysis examined whether defense styles explain incremental variance in BPTs beyond internalizing and externalizing symptoms in a clinical sample of 110 early adolescents aged 11-14 years. Participants completed the Borderline Personality Features Scale for Children, Youth Self-Report, and Defense Style Questionnaire-40. Associations were examined using correlations and hierarchical multiple regression. BPTs were strongly associated with internalizing symptoms (r = 0.72) and moderately with externalizing symptoms (r = 0.40); immature defenses showed the strongest bivariate association with BPTs (r = 0.56). Age, gender, internalizing, and externalizing symptoms explained 55.9% of BPT variance, increasing to 61.7% after adding defense styles (ΔR^2 = 0.058, p = 0.006, f^2 = 0.151). However, none of the individual defense style coefficients remained statistically significant after Holm correction. These findings indicate a modest but statistically significant incremental contribution of defense styles considered jointly, without establishing an independent association for any defense style.

items.title: Personal Social Capital on Depressive Symptoms Among College Students at a Medical University in China: The Moderated Mediating Role of Implicit Health Beliefs and Adverse Childhood Experiences.
items.authors: Lai X, Huang J, Yang H, Habibi S, Yan H, Zhang Y, Yang Y, Liu X.

sections.text: Depression is a major threat to college students' mental health, yet little is known about how external resources and internal assets jointly promote positive adaptation among young people exposed to adversity. This study examined whether implicit health beliefs mediate the association between personal social capital and depressive symptoms and whether adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) moderate these pathways. A total of 1910 Chinese college students completed the Personal Social Capital Scale-8 (PSCS-8), Lay Theories of Health Scale (LTHS), Revised Adverse Childhood Experience Questionnaire (ACEQ-R), and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using multiple regression. Personal social capital was negatively associated, with a direct effect of B = -0.220 ( p < 0.001) after accounting for implicit health beliefs. Implicit health beliefs partially mediated this association, accounting for 25.32% of the total effect. ACEs significantly moderated the associations between personal social capital and implicit health beliefs (B = 0.022, p < 0.001), personal social capital and depressive symptoms (B = -0.022, p < 0.05), and implicit health beliefs and depressive symptoms (B = 0.052, p < 0.05). These findings suggest that personal social capital, as an external resource, and implicit health beliefs, as an internal asset, were jointly associated with lower levels of depressive symptoms among risk-exposed youth. Strengthening supportive social resources and adaptive health beliefs may be relevant to resilience and inform youth mental health promotion and prevention strategies, particularly for students with adverse childhood experiences.

This study examined whether implicit health beliefs mediate the association between personal social capital and depressive symptoms and whether adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) moderate these pathways. A total of 1910 Chinese college students completed the Personal Social Capital Scale-8 (PSCS-8), Lay Theories of Health Scale (LTHS), Revised Adverse Childhood Experience Questionnaire (ACEQ-R), and Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9). Mediation and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using multiple regression. Personal social capital was negatively associated, with a direct effect of B = -0.220 ( p < 0.001) after accounting for implicit health beliefs. Implicit health beliefs partially mediated this association, accounting for 25.32% of the total effect. ACEs significantly moderated the associations between personal social capital and implicit health beliefs (B = 0.022, p < 0.001), personal social capital and depressive symptoms (B = -0.022, p < 0.05), and implicit health beliefs and depressive symptoms (B = 0.052, p < 0.05). These findings suggest that personal social capital, as an external resource, and implicit health beliefs, as an internal asset, were jointly associated with lower levels of depressive symptoms among risk-exposed youth. Strengthening supportive social resources and adaptive health beliefs may be relevant to resilience and inform youth mental health promotion and prevention strategies, particularly for students with adverse childhood experiences.

items.title: Preferred Gambling Modality and Hazardous Drinking Among Adults Screening Positive for Gambling Disorder: A Conceptual Replication from Türkiye.
items.authors: Arslan H, Tamam L.

sections.text: Mixed-mode gamblers, who gamble online and in physical venues, reportedly consume more alcohol while gambling than online-only gamblers in Australia, where many venues serve alcohol. This conceptual replication tested whether this pattern holds in Türkiye, where alcohol consumption is low, casinos are closed, and licensed betting shops do not serve alcohol. Cross-sectional data from 435 adults screening positive on the Turkish Gambling Disorder Screening Test (90.6% male) were analyzed. Hazardous drinking (Addiction Profile Index Risk Screening Scale, alcohol subscale) was compared across preferred gambling modality, tobacco use, and psychiatric diagnosis, adjusting for gambling disorder severity and sociodemographic characteristics. After adjustment, hazardous drinking differed by modality ( F (2, 418) = 16.94, p < 0.001, partial η^2 = 0.075). The mixed-mode group scored higher than the online group (adjusted difference = 1.84, 95% CI [1.21, 2.46]), and this difference remained among men and participants with past-year symptoms. Mixed-mode and land-based groups did not differ in the main model. Current tobacco users and participants without a psychiatric diagnosis also scored higher. The original finding was replicated in the direction where licensed venues do not sell alcohol. As 52.9% scored in the risk range, services could screen all clients for alcohol use, using modality and tobacco status as context.

items.title: Digital School-Based Social and Emotional Learning Interventions for Children and Adolescents: A Systematic Review of Randomized Controlled Trials with a Descriptive Comparison of Fully Digital and Blended Delivery.
items.authors: Gkora V, Galanaki E, Drigas A, Vassilakou T, Trimmi K, Merakou K.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Social and emotional learning (SEL) promotes children's social-emotional competencies and well-being, and educational technology offers new ways of delivering it. This systematic review evaluated digital school-based SEL interventions for children and adolescents, focusing on competencies of the Collaborative for Academic, Social, and Emotional Learning (CASEL) framework and mental health outcomes, and described how fully digital and blended programs differ in delivery and reported outcomes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, the Education Resources Information Center (ERIC), and Google Scholar were searched for randomized and cluster-randomized trials published between January 2015 and August 2026. Risk of bias was assessed with the revised Cochrane risk-of-bias tool (RoB 2), including its cluster-randomized extension; results were synthesized without meta-analysis following the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis (SWiM) guideline, using vote counting by effect direction, and certainty was rated with the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) approach.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Thirty-five trials (N = 15,026) were included; thirteen interventions were fully digital and twenty-two blended. Twenty-five trials reported a between-group advantage on at least one outcome. Only nine trials (26%) were prospectively registered. Coded by direction irrespective of statistical significance, all trials measuring composite social-emotional competence, relationship skills, or social awareness, and fourteen of fifteen measuring self-management, favoured the intervention. Certainty was moderate that the interventions probably improve composite social-emotional competence, low that they may improve the five CASEL competencies and well-being, and very low for emotional and behavioural difficulties, including anxiety and depressive symptoms, for which inconsistent results and risk-of-bias concerns limited confidence. No trial compared fully digital with blended delivery of the same program, and format overlapped with age, outcomes measured, and informant.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Digital school-based SEL interventions are a promising but still emerging approach. Whether human support enhances their effects remains untested, and the low rate of prospective trial registration limits confidence in the evidence.

items.title: The role of basic psychological need satisfaction in the relationship between exercise and well-being in adolescents: a systematic review.
items.authors: Chen S, Chen T, Chen T.
items.journal: Frontiers in child and adolescent psychiatry

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Over recent decades, global adolescent wellbeing has deteriorated, with around 13.4% of adolescents worldwide meeting diagnostic criteria for at least one mental disorder. Although physical activity enhances adolescent wellbeing, the mechanisms driving this effect remain only partially understood. This systematic review examines whether basic psychological need satisfaction (BPNS-autonomy, competence, relatedness) mediates the relationship between exercise and wellbeing among 10-18-year-olds.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We systematically searched five electronic databases for peer-reviewed studies published between 2000 and 2026. In total, 23 studies met our inclusion criteria; these studies were narratively synthesized, assessed for risk of bias via design-appropriate tools, and collectively encompassed over 10,000 adolescents from 13 countries.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Elevated BPNS was consistently linked to higher subjective vitality, greater life satisfaction, increased positive affect, and enhanced flourishing ( β  = 0.19-0.80; r  = 0.19-0.68). Competence satisfaction emerged as the most reliable predictor of wellbeing, especially in competitive sports, while autonomy and relatedness impacts varied by context. Psychological need frustration independently associated with negative affect and burnout, supporting the dual-process model. Evidence is most robust in school physical education contexts, with notably scarce research on mindfulness-based and resistance training. The only included cluster-randomized controlled trial reported no significant intervention effect, and reliance on observational designs constrains causal inference.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This review highlights BPNS-especially competence satisfaction-as a credible mechanism linking exercise to better adolescent wellbeing. Thus, physical education curricula, youth sports initiatives, and exercise programs should adopt need-supportive approaches. Future RCTs must pre-specify BPNS as a mediator to confirm causal pathways.

items.title: Systematic review of quantitative studies exploring links between mindfulness, mental health, and social media use.
items.authors: Jones CA, Tibber MS.

sections.text: There is growing interest in inter-individual differences linked to risk and resilience in the associations between social media use and mental health. Here, we systematically reviewed empirical studies exploring links between mindfulness, social media use, and mental health, in order to explore the possibility that mindfulness plays a protective role. Systematic searches of PsychInfo, Medline, and Web of Science databases were run from database inception to January 2026. Forty-three studies met criteria for inclusion. Mindfulness was modelled variably as an independent variable, dependent variable, mediator, and moderator. Overwhelmingly, results linked mindfulness to better mental health and more beneficial patterns of social media use, and mediated/ moderated associations between the two in a protective manner where tested. Existing studies were limited by a predominance of cross-sectional designs, a paucity of research in non-'WEIRD' samples, and a bias towards younger population samples. The findings support the role of mindfulness as a potential protective factor in the association between social media and mental health, but highlight a need for longitudinal and experimental research to unpick underlying directions of causality, and examine the clinical utility of mindfulness as a modifiable trait.

items.title: Screen-Printed Carbon Electrode-Based Biosensors for Mental Health Biomarker Monitoring: Current Advances, Challenges and AI-Integrated Future Perspectives.
items.authors: Selvarajan RS, Nathan A, Yaghoubi E, Maghami MR, Yaghoubi E, Menon PS.

sections.text: The need for rapid and early mental health monitoring remains unmet as conventional diagnostic approaches still rely heavily on episodic measurements and subjective assessment tools. Electrochemical biosensors have emerged as one of the promising solutions to address this gap as they offer rapid, sensitive and minimally invasive detection of biomarkers related to stress, anxiety and depression. Among the diverse sensing platforms, screen-printed carbon electrodes (SPCEs) are attractive due to low cost, disposability, portability, easy surface modification, and compatibility with wearables and point-of-care applications. This review critically evaluates SPCE-based electrochemical biosensors for mental health biomarker monitoring. Specifically, this review synthesizes evidence across target biomarkers, biological sample matrices, detection techniques, surface functionalization strategies and nanomaterial-based signal enhancement. However, translational barriers such as biofouling, matrix interference, signal drift, limited standardized protocols, and insufficient large-scale clinical validation are identified as the key limiting factors for real-world deployment. Comparative analysis reveals that cortisol targeting SPCE platforms are currently the most clinically advanced, whereas multiplexed biomarker detection with AI integration provides a promising avenue for future development. Overall, this review establishes SPCE-based biosensing technology as the key platform for developing next-generation objective and scalable mental health monitoring devices with a proposed future direction roadmap toward AI-integrated clinical translation.

items.title: Psychometric properties of the Danish PSS-10 in adolescents.
items.authors: Steen PB, Mors O, Dalgaard VL, Sørensen CLB, Andersen JH, Biering K.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: The 10-item Perceived Stress Scale (PSS-10) is widely used internationally, but its measurement properties have not been evaluated in Danish adolescents. The aim of this study was to assess the structural, construct, and criterion validity, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and measurement precision of the Danish PSS-10, and to explore its ability to discriminate between adolescents with and without clinically assessed psychiatric diagnoses.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A random sample of 5,699 adolescents aged 15-20 years was invited to participate. Of these, 667 completed the PSS-10 questionnaire in the first round (test sample), and 182 completed it a second time after approximately one week (retest sample). Structural validity was assessed using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using one- and two-factor models. Internal consistency was evaluated using Cronbach's alpha. Test-retest reliability (n = 182) was evaluated using intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and the standard error of measurement (SEM). Construct and criterion validity was assessed in a subsample (n = 38) who completed a Schedules for Clinical Assessment in Neuropsychiatry (SCAN) interview. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis was used to examine the discriminative ability of the PSS-10 in relation to clinically assessed psychiatric diagnoses and to explore a potential threshold score.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The two-factor model showed the best statistical fit, although the overall pattern of findings supported use of the total PSS-10 score. Internal consistency was excellent, as indicated by a Cronbach's alpha = 0.90. Test-retest reliability was high with a ICC(2,1) = 0.89 and SEM = 2.65 resulting in a minimal detectable change of 7.34, which corresponds to an 18% change in score. The PSS-10 score showed strong correlations with psychiatric symptom scores, supporting construct validity. The ROC analysis showed good discriminative ability (AUC = 0.88). Exploratory analyses identified a threshold score of ≥ 24 that optimally discriminated between adolescents with and without a psychiatric diagnosis.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: The Danish PSS-10 demonstrated good structural validity, internal consistency, test-retest reliability, measurement precision, and construct and criterion validity in adolescents. The findings support the use of the total PSS-10 score for assessing perceived stress in this population. Exploratory analyses suggested a potential threshold score of ≥ 24, however larger validation studies are needed before this threshold can be recommended.

sections.text: The data collection was registered and approved by the regional register of research projects (#788218) on 3 January 2023.

items.title: Male Suicidality and Fractured Intimate Relationships: The Lived Experience of Men.
items.authors: Arrigo JL, Fitzpatrick S, McCormack L.

sections.text: Intimate relationship difficulties are associated with men's suicidality, yet how men make sense of these experiences remains insufficiently understood. This interpretative phenomenological analysis explored the retrospective accounts of eight Australian men who had attempted suicide in the context of perceived intimate relationship problems. An overarching theme, The Burden of Chronic Intimate Disillusionment, encompassed six group experiential themes. Participants described the importance of intimate relationships to belonging, purpose and self-worth, alongside experiences of emotional disconnection, earlier adversity, perceived nonreciprocity and compromised boundaries. Accounts varied: some described abrupt separation, whereas others understood their distress as accumulating alongside illness, financial hardship or social isolation. Some participants described their caring and provider roles as integral to who they were, making disruption to these roles especially painful; other accounts admitted mutual difficulties or questioned their own expectations. Suicidal crises were retrospectively associated with overwhelming psychological pain, entrapment and a perceived inability to envisage alternatives. Subsequent meaning-making included renegotiated boundaries and sources of worth beyond the previous relationship, although trust in future intimacy was not necessarily restored. Altruistic identity disruption and the integrated motivational-volitional model offer possible interpretations of participants' experiences for future research. Findings suggest the value of directly exploring men's relational meanings, isolation and identity investment in suicide prevention, while recognising the limitations of a selected, retrospective, single-perspective sample.

items.title: Longitudinal Non-Pharmacological Neuromodulation and Cognitive Training Across Sequential Intervention Studies in a Participant with Alzheimer's Disease: A 10-Year Single-Participant Analysis.
items.authors: Moussavi Z, Uehara MA, Garcia-Campuzano M.

sections.text: Objectives: Non-pharmacological interventions for Alzheimer's disease (AD) are typically studied as single modalities over months; long-term, multi-modal outcome data in one individual, of clear relevance to the psychiatric care of older adults with dementia over time, are rare. We describe the cognitive trajectory of one participant who, over 10 years, took part sequentially in five non-invasive AD intervention studies, and place his cognitive change in the context of decline rates reported in published AD cohorts. Methods: Retrospective, single-participant analysis integrating data from a university research laboratory (University of Manitoba, Canada; 2013-2025) across five sequential protocols: virtual-reality (VR) navigational neurorehabilitation; a randomized trial of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS); cognitive training with/without 40 Hz transcranial alternating current stimulation (tACS); a crossover sham-controlled tACS study; and an ongoing personalized-frequency tACS/tDCS study. The participant was one male, healthy at 2013 enrollment, later diagnosed with mild cognitive impairment (2016) and AD (2018), who received no pharmacological AD treatment. Interventions included VR spatial navigation training; bilateral DLPFC rTMS; 40 Hz and personalized gamma/theta tACS/tDCS over left DLPFC paired with cognitive exercises; and intermittent cognitive-training-only blocks. Outcomes were assessed with the MoCA, ADAS-Cog, Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire, and VR navigation error. Long-term ADAS-Cog change was quantified with linear regression (slope, 95% CI) for the intervention and post-intervention periods, with sensitivity and segmented (interrupted time-series) analyses. Results: Over the ~5.4-year intervention period (November 2018-April 2024), which comprised 12 four-week intervention blocks separated by treatment-free intervals, ADAS-Cog fluctuated between 12.3 and 23.0 but showed no significant long-term trend (slope +0.32 points/year; 95% CI -0.25 to 0.89). Published group-level data suggest a decline of approximately 10-12 points over a comparable interval. ADAS-Cog was higher at the two latest assessments after treatment ended (22.0 and 22.3), but these values were within the range observed during intervention, and post-intervention data were too sparse to estimate a reliable trend. MoCA was 21 in 2018 and 2021, 19 in October 2022, and 13 in March 2025; when the latter decline occurred within that interval cannot be determined. Conclusions: In this single participant, a period of repeated, intermittent non-invasive brain stimulation combined with cognitive training was temporally associated with a flat long-term ADAS-Cog trajectory, slower than published group-level decline rates. Because the design is retrospective and uncontrolled, these observations cannot establish the efficacy of any intervention or attribute later changes to treatment cessation. They are hypothesis-generating, relevant to clinicians managing long-term cognitive care in dementia, and support controlled studies of long-term individualized non-invasive brain stimulation with cognitive training.

Conclusions: In this single participant, a period of repeated, intermittent non-invasive brain stimulation combined with cognitive training was temporally associated with a flat long-term ADAS-Cog trajectory, slower than published group-level decline rates. Because the design is retrospective and uncontrolled, these observations cannot establish the efficacy of any intervention or attribute later changes to treatment cessation. They are hypothesis-generating, relevant to clinicians managing long-term cognitive care in dementia, and support controlled studies of long-term individualized non-invasive brain stimulation with cognitive training.

items.title: Autistic Traits and Orthorexic Tendencies in Patients with Eating Disorders: An Exploratory Study.
items.authors: Carpita B, Nardi B, Pini S, Pronestì C, Giovannoni F, Parri F, Massimetti G, Cremone IM, Bruno A, Luciano M, Muscatello MRA, Fiorillo A, Dell'Osso L.

sections.text: Background: This study aimed to investigate the relationship between orthorexic tendencies, autistic traits (ATs), and eating disorder (ED) psychopathology in patients with anorexia nervosa (AN), bulimia nervosa (BN), and binge eating disorder (BED), compared to healthy controls (HCs). Methods: A total of 125 participants were assessed using the Adult Autism Subthreshold Spectrum (AdAS Spectrum), ORTO-15, and Eating Disorder Inventory-2 (EDI-2). Results: ED patients exhibited significantly greater orthorexic tendencies and higher AdAS Spectrum and EDI-2 scores than HCs. ORTO-15 scores were significantly associated with both AdAS Spectrum and EDI-2 total scores and with most of their respective domains. In the multivariable regression model, AdAS Spectrum total score was significantly associated with orthorexic tendencies, whereas EDI-2 total score did not reach statistical significance. However, within the EDI-2 domains, Drive for Thinness and Maturity Fears were significantly associated with greater orthorexic tendencies. Among the AdAS Spectrum domains, Non-Verbal Communication was significantly associated with greater orthorexic tendencies. Conclusions: Orthorexic tendencies were elevated among ED patients and were associated with ATs and ED symptomatology itself. Our findings highlight the potential relevance of AT in understanding orthorexic tendencies in patients with ED and warrant confirmation in larger studies using psychometrically refined measures of orthorexia.

items.title: Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling and Simulation of Quetiapine in Chinese Psychiatric Patients for Individualized Dosing and Missed-Dose Management.
items.authors: Li Y, Huang S, Lu H, Xia H, Yan H, Huang W, Yan X, Zhang M, Xia S, Shang D.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: To develop a population pharmacokinetic (PPK) model for quetiapine using real-world therapeutic drug monitoring (TDM) data from psychiatric patients, evaluate the influence of demographic characteristics, pharmacogenetic factors, and concomitant medications on quetiapine pharmacokinetics, and develop model-informed remedial dosing strategies for missed-dose scenarios.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A retrospective PPK analysis was conducted using TDM data from patients receiving quetiapine. Population pharmacokinetic analysis was performed using nonlinear mixed-effects modeling (NONMEM). Demographic variables, CYP2D6 polymorphisms, and concomitant medications were evaluated as candidate covariates. Model performance was assessed using goodness-of-fit plots, bootstrap analysis, and normalized prediction distribution errors (NPDE). Model simulations were performed to evaluate quetiapine exposure in representative patient populations and to investigate remedial dosing strategies following delayed or missed doses.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 986 TDM concentrations from 210 psychiatric patients were included. Quetiapine pharmacokinetics were described by a one-compartment model with first-order absorption and elimination. The estimated apparent clearance (CL/F) and apparent volume of distribution (V/F) were 107 L/h and 2090 L, respectively. Age and concomitant sertraline use were retained as significant covariates during the predefined covariate modeling procedure. Model simulations suggested that these covariates influenced quetiapine exposure profiles. Missed doses resulted in rapid declines in serum concentrations below the selected therapeutic reference range, whereas model-informed remedial dosing strategies improved target attainment while limiting excessive concentration fluctuations.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: A population pharmacokinetic model describing quetiapine pharmacokinetics in psychiatric patients was successfully developed using real-world TDM data. Model-informed simulations suggest that this framework may support individualized dose optimization and the evaluation of remedial dosing strategies following missed doses.

items.title: Age-stratified reporting patterns of medications and suicide-related events in FAERS.
items.authors: Zhang H, Diao J, Liu L.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Recent studies have demonstrated that multiple commonly prescribed medications are associated with suicide-related events. However, existing research lacks stratified statistical analysis between minors and adults, potentially obscuring age-specific risks.

sections.heading: Objectives
sections.text: To conduct a descriptive assessment of reporting patterns across different age groups.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Using the Reporting Odds Ratio (ROR) method and Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network (BCPNN) method, we analyzed data from the U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) database. This analysis identified drugs from various categories reported by healthcare professionals and associated with 9 preferred terms related to "suicide-related adverse events."

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 164,707 reports of suicide-related incidents were identified. stratification by age revealed differences in the types of drugs associated with suicidal ideation across age groups. Among minors, the top two drugs linked to suicidal ideation were isotretinoin (n=426 cases) and montelukast (n=351 cases), whereas in adults, the highest-ranked drugs were sertraline (n=569 cases) and quetiapine (n=529 cases). However, regarding completed suicide reports, acetaminophen was the most frequently reported medication for both minors and adults.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study found that different types of suicide-related adverse events vary in age distribution and drug category.

items.title: Demonstration of how group model building can be used to understand barriers and facilitators to "at-risk" young people's access to community assets for mental health support: a participatory study.
items.authors: Fisher H, Er V, Longdon B, Gnani S, Hartwell G, Keenan M, Mutanda D, Robinson H, Dodd H, Kidger J.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Community assets (e.g. green spaces, youth centres) can support the mental health of young people. However, less is known about barriers and facilitators to access these assets. This manuscript aims to demonstrate how group model building - a participatory research method grounded in systems thinking - can be used to examine the ways in which community assets support the mental health of "at-risk" young people, while identifying the barriers and facilitators that shape access to these assets.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Community-based recruitment was undertaken in rural towns and two urban areas in the South of England. Participants included young people, parents/carers and decision-makers/practitioners. Each group took part in two workshops per site, during which systems maps were developed to visually represent the dynamic interrelationships (feedback loops) within the system. In total, nine group-specific systems maps (one per participant group in each site) were produced and synthesized into a single merged systems map to identify shared patterns and key leverage points.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: A total of 32 young people aged 14-16 years (identified as "at-risk" by local services or self-identification), 31 parents/carers and 31 decision-makers/practitioners participated in 20 workshops conducted between May and July 2025. Four key feedback loops were identified: (1) increased investment in prevention and early intervention services enhances access to appropriate activities and improves wellbeing; (2) competition for limited resources can reduce staff capacity to deliver services and impacts on sustainability; (3) access to community assets promotes personal development and emotional support through engagement with trusted adults and structured activities; and (4) experiences of discrimination reduce young people's sense of belonging, limiting their use of public spaces and negatively impacting their emotional wellbeing.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Group model building provides a novel and participatory approach to generating shared understanding of how community assets support the mental health of "at-risk" young people. Potential areas for action to address inequalities and improve young people's mental health nationally include securing resources for prevention and early intervention services, increasing presence of trusted adults in public spaces, enhancing quality of community assets and youth provision offer and improving awareness of existing services.

items.title: The Role of Psychostimulants in the Management of Refractory Catatonia: A Comprehensive Review of Case Reports.
items.authors: Margoni S, Onori L, Kotzalidis GD, Pinto M, Montanari S, Bartolucci G, Koukopoulos AE, Pellegrino M, Moccia L, Simonetti A, Sani G, Janiri D.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Catatonia is a neuropsychiatric syndrome characterised by motor, behavioural, and affective abnormalities and is frequently associated with mood disorders, particularly major depressive and bipolar disorders. Although benzodiazepines and electroconvulsive therapy are considered first-line treatments, a substantial proportion of patients show partial or no response, especially in chronic, affective, or medically complex presentations. Contemporary neurobiological models implicate dysfunction across multiple neurotransmitter systems, including GABAergic, glutamatergic, and dopaminergic pathways, as well as disturbances in cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical circuits involved in psychomotor control and arousal regulation. Within this framework, psychostimulants may exert therapeutic effects by enhancing dopaminergic and noradrenergic transmission, thereby modulating frontal-striatal networks and facilitating behavioural activation and motor initiation. Evidence from conditions characterised by psychomotor slowing, apathy, and impaired behavioural initiation provides a neurophysiological rationale for their adjunctive use in selected cases of catatonia, particularly when associated with mood disorders. However, there is a dearth of empirical data, with the evidence largely confined to case reports, hence the need for comprehensive reviews of cases and controlled studies to clarify the role of psychostimulants and to explore drug combinations in the treatment of catatonia. Methods: We conducted a comprehensive review of case reports on 22 October 2026 on PubMed, Scopus, PsycInfo/PsycArticles, and Web of Science. Results: We included 9 studies. Psychostimulants were usually helpful in inducing rapid symptoms resolution of catatonia. Conclusions: Psychostimulants may be used in cases of catatonia and provide rapid improvement. Future longitudinal, double-blind designs are likely to allow reliably assessing the value of psychostimulants in catatonia.

items.title: Fixed Body, Manageable Future: Making Sense of Epigenetic Mental Health Risks in Children.
items.authors: Shinomiya S, Shineha R.

sections.text: Epigenetic mental health testing is emerging as a technology for identifying children's vulnerability to future mental health conditions. Although ethical and social implications of epigenetics have been discussed, little is known about how people with lived experiences make sense of epigenetic mental health risk. We conducted four focus group interviews with 29 participants in Japan, including parents of children with past mental health difficulties and young adults who had experienced mental health difficulties in childhood. Data were analysed using reflexive thematic analysis. Participants rarely understood epigenetic risk as information about future disease alone. Instead, they interpreted it as knowledge about personhood, revealing what kind of person one is through familiar local concepts such as tokusei (characteristics). Whereas scientific accounts emphasise biological plasticity, participants relocated plasticity not to the biological characteristics themselves but to futures resulting from those relatively fixed characteristics. Likewise, risk was relocated from disease risk itself to the consequences of acting upon epigenetic knowledge, such as limiting one's potential through a deterministic understanding of test results. These findings demonstrate that epigenetic risk is translated into familiar frameworks rather than simply transmitted from science to society, with important implications for the communication and implementation of emerging epigenetic testing.

items.title: Identifying mental health problems and pathways for intervention in the Roma community of Polígono Sur, Spain: a qualitative socio‑ecological study.
items.authors: March K, Barroso-Manzano JM, Mediavilla R, Moreno FJP, Bau-Dasí PF, Hernández CP, Poštuvan V, Hegerl U, Crespo-Facorro B, Ayuso-Mateos JL, McGreevy KR.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Roma communities in Spain experience disproportionate exposure to adverse social determinants of health, contributing to increased vulnerability to mental health problems. Despite these factors, scientific data on the mental health of the Roma population in Spain remains scarce. This study aimed to identify key mental health problems among Roma individuals of Polígono Sur, a highly disadvantaged neighbourhood in Seville, Spain; examine their perceived causes, consequences, and response strategies; and assess implications for developing culturally appropriate and community‑responsive mental health programmes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We conducted a two‑phase qualitative study following the Programme Design, Implementation, Monitoring, and Evaluation (DIME) protocol. In phase one, Free List (FL) interviews with 34 participants identified locally relevant problems. In phase two, 16 Key Informant (KI) interviews provided detailed descriptions of these problems, explored perceived causes and effects, and identified strategies considered useful to address them. Data were analysed using thematic analysis and organised within a five‑level socioecological framework (intrapersonal, interpersonal, organisational, community, and public policy).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Across FL interviews, we identified 74 problems affecting the Roma population in Polígono Sur and we explored the following problems in the KI: fear and insecurity, interpersonal conflict, isolation, and hopelessness. Perceived determinants and consequences emerged across all socioecological levels, underscoring the interplay among individual vulnerabilities, community dynamics, and structural disadvantage. Although several initiatives existed-primarily at the organisational level-substantial mental health needs remained unmet, particularly those related to community conditions, structural barriers, and policy gaps.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Findings highlight the need for mental health strategies within the Roma community that integrate individual‑level support with broader community‑centred and structural interventions. Based on our findings, we recommend adopting intercultural, preventive, and rights‑based approaches, complemented by culturally adapted self‑help materials and guided self‑help tools to strengthen coping skills, resilience, and stress management. Embedding these personal‑level supports within coordinated community and policy actions may provide a more comprehensive and sustainable response to the multi‑level mental health needs identified in this highly vulnerable population.

items.title: Manganese Transporter Genes and Environmental Exposure in Neurodevelopmental Disorders: Integrating Genetic, Epidemiological, and Experimental Evidence.
items.authors: Wang X, Li J, Wang M, Zhang Y, Yang X, Liu Q, Chang X, Wang H.

sections.text: Manganese (Mn) is an essential trace element, but both insufficient cellular availability and excessive accumulation can disrupt neurological function. This narrative review integrates evidence from inherited Mn transporter disorders, common genetic variation, environmental epidemiology, and experimental models to examine potential links at the gene-environment interface. Biallelic pathogenic variants in SLC39A8, SLC30A10, and SLC39A14 provide direct human evidence that impaired Mn uptake, utilization, or clearance can cause distinct neurological and neurodevelopmental phenotypes. Environmental Mn studies in children mainly report associations with cognitive, motor, attentional, and behavioral outcomes, but findings vary according to exposure timing, biomarker, sex, nutritional status, co-exposure, and outcome definition. Evidence linking environmental Mn specifically to attention deficit hyperactivity disorder or autism spectrum disorder remains heterogeneous and observational. Experimental data suggest that Mn deficiency and excess involve partly distinct mechanisms, including altered glycosylation, mitochondrial and cellular dysfunction, iron-redox imbalance, ferroptosis-related responses, glial activation, and epigenetic or transcriptional changes. However, a causal Mn-epigenetic-neurodevelopmental pathway and a generalizable gene-environment interaction have not been established in humans. Advancing this field will require studies that integrate time-resolved exposure assessment, genetic and nutritional stratification, multi-omics, neuroimaging, and functional models.

items.title: Clinical and Genetic Characterization of Preschool Girls with Autism Spectrum Disorder: Insights from Copy Number Variants and X-Chromosome Inactivation.
items.authors: Graziano RT, Bernardini L, Giovannone F, Pizzuti A, Sogos C.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Females remain underrepresented in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) research. We characterized clinical and genetic profiles of preschool girls with ASD, focusing on copy number variants (CNVs) and X-chromosome inactivation (XCI).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Thirty-two girls with ASD (mean age 3.18 ± 0.85 years) underwent standardized assessment, chromosomal microarray analysis, FMR1 testing, and XCI evaluation using a methylation-sensitive androgen receptor assay. Clinical features were compared between participants with at least one reportable CNV and those with no reportable CNV detected. Identified CNVs were retrospectively reassessed according to ACMG/ClinGen standards. Multiple-testing correction and a sensitivity analysis comparing pathogenic/VUS CNV carriers with participants showing no reportable CNV or only likely benign CNVs were performed.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Developmental impairment was frequent, with 24/32 participants (75.0%) showing a GMDS-III developmental quotient below 70. At least one reportable CNV was identified in 14/32 participants (43.8%), and 18/32 (56.3%) had none. Following expert reassessment according to ACMG/ClinGen standards, 17 CNVs were classified as pathogenic ( n = 2), variants of uncertain significance ( n = 7), or likely benign ( n = 8). Pathogenic CNVs were identified in two participants (6.3% of the cohort). Among 25 participants informative for XCI, 24 (96.0%) showed non-markedly skewed XCI and one (4.0%) showed highly skewed XCI (7:93). In primary analyses based on original reportable-CNV status, nominal differences were observed for ADOS-2 symptom severity and sleep difficulties, but these did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction. Continuous GMDS-III, VABS-II, and DP-3 scores did not differ significantly between groups. Primary cross-sectional phenotype-CNV associations did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. In the exploratory CBCL 6-18 follow-up analyses, differences in Externalizing Problems, Total Problems, and DSM-oriented Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Problems remained significant after FDR correction under the original reportable-CNV grouping, but none remained significant in the sensitivity analysis based on CNV reclassification.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Highly skewed XCI was uncommon in this cohort, whereas pathogenic CNVs were identified in a minority of participants despite the relatively high frequency of reportable genomic findings. Primary cross-sectional clinical differences did not survive multiple-testing correction, and phenotype-CNV associations were further attenuated after CNV reclassification. These findings underscore the heterogeneity of female ASD and support a cautious interpretation of genotype-phenotype associations based solely on the presence of reportable CNVs.

abstract.text:
Females remain underrepresented in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) research. We characterized clinical and genetic profiles of preschool girls with ASD, focusing on copy number variants (CNVs) and X-chromosome inactivation (XCI).

Thirty-two girls with ASD (mean age 3.18 ± 0.85 years) underwent standardized assessment, chromosomal microarray analysis, FMR1 testing, and XCI evaluation using a methylation-sensitive androgen receptor assay. Clinical features were compared between participants with at least one reportable CNV and those with no reportable CNV detected. Identified CNVs were retrospectively reassessed according to ACMG/ClinGen standards. Multiple-testing correction and a sensitivity analysis comparing pathogenic/VUS CNV carriers with participants showing no reportable CNV or only likely benign CNVs were performed.

Developmental impairment was frequent, with 24/32 participants (75.0%) showing a GMDS-III developmental quotient below 70. At least one reportable CNV was identified in 14/32 participants (43.8%), and 18/32 (56.3%) had none. Following expert reassessment according to ACMG/ClinGen standards, 17 CNVs were classified as pathogenic ( n = 2), variants of uncertain significance ( n = 7), or likely benign ( n = 8). Pathogenic CNVs were identified in two participants (6.3% of the cohort). Among 25 participants informative for XCI, 24 (96.0%) showed non-markedly skewed XCI and one (4.0%) showed highly skewed XCI (7:93). In primary analyses based on original reportable-CNV status, nominal differences were observed for ADOS-2 symptom severity and sleep difficulties, but these did not remain significant after false discovery rate correction. Continuous GMDS-III, VABS-II, and DP-3 scores did not differ significantly between groups. Primary cross-sectional phenotype-CNV associations did not remain significant after multiple-testing correction. In the exploratory CBCL 6-18 follow-up analyses, differences in Externalizing Problems, Total Problems, and DSM-oriented Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Problems remained significant after FDR correction under the original reportable-CNV grouping, but none remained significant in the sensitivity analysis based on CNV reclassification.

Highly skewed XCI was uncommon in this cohort, whereas pathogenic CNVs were identified in a minority of participants despite the relatively high frequency of reportable genomic findings. Primary cross-sectional clinical differences did not survive multiple-testing correction, and phenotype-CNV associations were further attenuated after CNV reclassification. These findings underscore the heterogeneity of female ASD and support a cautious interpretation of genotype-phenotype associations based solely on the presence of reportable CNVs.

items.title: Barriers to Seeking Physical and Mental Health Care Among Healthcare Students in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.authors: Almogheer WS, Alotaibi AF, Alanazi AS, Alanazi AS, BinArbeed KM.

sections.text: Background Medical students face high levels of stress and depression during training, increasing medical errors and impairing performance. However, few students seek professional help, often self-medicating or relying on peers because of stigma, confidentiality concerns, limited awareness of available services, fear of intervention, and lack of time. Methods A cross-sectional, self-administered online survey was conducted among healthcare students enrolled in Medicine, Dentistry, and Pharmacy courses at King Saud bin Abdulaziz University for Health Sciences and King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, from September 9, 2025, to July 1, 2026. Students were selected by stratified random sampling and invited by email (2,000 invitations); 482 students completed the 28-item Barriers to Health Care Seeking Questionnaire (14 matched mental and physical healthcare item pairs, five-point response scale, positively worded items reverse-scored) together with sociodemographic and health-related questions. Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics for Windows, version 27 (IBM Corp., Armonk, New York, United States). Descriptive statistics and Cronbach's alpha were calculated; mental and physical barrier scores were compared using the paired-samples t test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test (Cohen's dz); scores across colleges were compared using Welch's analysis of variance and the Kruskal-Wallis test with post hoc tests; and independent predictors were identified using multivariable linear regression. P values were adjusted for multiple comparisons (Holm procedure), with two-tailed significance set at p<0.05 and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) reported. Results Among the 482 participants (mean age 21.68 years) studying medicine (72.8%), dentistry (14.5%), and pharmacy (12.7%), mental health care barriers exceeded physical health care barriers by a mean of 4.11 points (95% CI 3.56-4.66, p<0.001), and 66.2% scored higher on the mental health barriers subscale. Lack of time was the most commonly reported barrier (70.1%), followed by cost (35.8%) and uncertainty about where to seek help (33.3%). The greatest mental-physical care gaps involved fear of harming grades/career prospects, confidentiality, perceived lack of benefit of consultation, and reluctance to see a known clinician. Physical health care barriers varied significantly across colleges and were lowest among medical students; mental health care barriers did not differ across colleges. Only college of study was independently associated with physical health barriers, and not with mental health barriers. Conclusion Healthcare students at two universities in Riyadh perceived greater barriers to mental health care than to physical health care, and this gap was accompanied by higher perceived confidentiality, career concerns, and clinician familiarity, alongside widespread time constraints. This suggests that structural changes, such as separating health services from academic assessment and strengthening confidentiality-related policies, are potential strategies that warrant further evaluation.

items.title: Determinants of Teachers' Psychosocial Challenges in South African Secondary Schools: A Scoping Review.
items.authors: Mpyana NB, Ndlovu SM, Makofane IB, Themane MJ, Mabasa LT, Buthelezi MM.

sections.text: Teachers face significant psychosocial challenges worsened by heavy workloads and inadequate mental health support. These challenges, including stress, burnout, anxiety and depression negatively impact both teachers and learners. This scoping review aimed to identify determinants of psychosocial challenges among secondary school teachers in South Africa over 2020-2025. Guided by the Arksey and O'Malley framework, a comprehensive search was conducted across five databases (EBSCOhost, PubMed, Sabinet, ScienceDirect and ProQuest), supplemented by Google Scholar citation tracking and backward reference searching of the included studies. Reporting followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews, and the findings were interpreted through self-determination theory (SDT). Eleven studies were included in the final synthesis. This review identified workload, violence and school culture as primary determinants compromising psychosocial well-being. Teachers face excessive workloads, physical and emotional violence from learners, and a lack of safety and supportive leadership. Addressing teacher mental health is essential for improving educational outcomes and a fundamental human right. The findings have implications for South African education, such as the need for more available staff psychosocial support services for teachers, stronger implementation of school safety and learner support frameworks and supportive school leadership. Systemic interventions, beyond individual stress management programmes, are urgently needed to mitigate psychosocial challenges and create supportive school environments. This review underscores the importance of prioritising teacher well-being as a cornerstone of a healthy education system.

items.title: Assessment of online mental health content: integrating lightweight language models with clinical quality criteria.
items.authors: Javed H, Ayadi M, Oh H, Ali F.

sections.text: The rapid expansion of online mental health information has created major challenges in sustaining content quality and ensuring user safety and public health outcomes. Manual review processes cannot keep pace with the increasing volume of digital material, and existing automated tools often lack the capacity to deliver comprehensive clinical evaluations. To address these gaps, we introduce an automated domain-specific criterion-based framework that integrates quality assessment criterion for lightweight language models to evaluate mental health content across 20 clinically relevant criteria, including reliability, information safety, cultural sensitivity, and adequacy of crisis-related resources. The models are evaluated on a curated corpus of 416 educational articles from seven authoritative institutional sources. Within this setting, the study focuses on criterion-level quality assessment of institutional educational content and provides a foundation for later extension to commercially biased and adversarial material. Clinical validation shows strong agreement with expert review (89% of high-scoring articles meeting informational standards; model-expert κ = 0.78, n = 100). By enhancing reliability, supporting safer digital health practices, the framework will further support researchers in mental health quality assessment using lightweight language models and has the potential to strengthen the trustworthiness, clinical utility, and public health impact of digital mental health resources.

items.authors: Cui J, Zeng Y.

items.title: A Previously Unreported POU3F3 p.(Lys409Ter) Variant in Snijders Blok-Fisher Syndrome: Mechanistic Context of Expressed Truncating Alleles.
items.authors: Yang L, Chen M.

sections.text: Background: Snijders Blok-Fisher syndrome (SNIBFIS; OMIM #618604) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder associated with heterozygous POU3F3 variants and characterized by developmental delay, prominent speech and language impairment, behavioral abnormalities, and dysmorphic features. Case Presentation: We report a Chinese boy evaluated at 7 years and 9 months for longstanding developmental and language delay. He walked independently at 18 months, began using meaningful single words at approximately 24 months, and remained unable to produce complete sentences at 7 years of age. Wechsler intelligence testing yielded a full-scale IQ of 57. Clinical evaluation documented attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder and autism spectrum disorder, with a Childhood Autism Rating Scale score of 38. Additional findings included sleep-onset difficulty, low-set ears, an open-mouth appearance, a single transverse palmar crease, and left hyperopia. He had no history of seizures, and electroencephalography was normal. Trio whole-exome sequencing identified a heterozygous POU3F3 nonsense variant, NM_006236.3:c.1225A>T [p.(Lys409Ter)], absent from both parental blood samples and reported as de novo by the diagnostic laboratory. The variant was not identified in the published literature or publicly accessible variant resources searched through 8 September 2026. Conclusions: This case adds to the reported POU3F3 variant spectrum and illustrates the importance of considering the unusual behavior of truncating alleles in this intronless gene.

items.title: Autosomal Copy Number Variants in Neurodevelopmental Disorders Phenotypes: A 5-Year Retrospective Study.
items.authors: Randazzo M, Cirnigliaro L, Saccuzzo L, Marzà V, Di Franco M, Vizzini GM, Romano C, Fichera M, Rizzo R, Barone R.

sections.text: Background: Microdeletion/microduplication syndromes are rare chromosomal abnormalities causing diverse clinical features due to gene dosage imbalances caused by submicroscopic deletions/duplications (Copy Number Variations-CNVs) of contiguous genes in specific chromosomal regions. CNVs causing microdeletion/microduplication syndromes encoded in reference databases (Orphanet, OMIM) have a significant clinical impact in neurodevelopmental disorders (NDDs). Methods: A retrospective study analyzed the molecular and clinical data of 446 pediatric patients referred for suspected NDDs to the Outpatient Clinic of the Child Neuropsychiatry Unit at University Hospital of Catania Italy, between 2020 and 2024. Final clinical diagnoses reflect comprehensive post-intake evaluations. Results: Over 446 patients, 156 (35%) had CNVs in autosomal chromosomes. Thirty-nine (8.7%), 28 males (71.8%) and 11 females (28.2%), with a mean age of 11.8 years (SD: 4.6), were diagnosed with microdeletion/microduplication syndromes. Chromosome 16 (30.8%, 12/39), chromosome 22 (12.8%, 5/39), chromosome 15 (7.7%, 3/39) and chromosome 7 (7.7%, 3/39) were more frequently implicated. De novo rearrangements accounted for 23.1% of cases (9/39), while 69.2% (27/39; 11 maternal, 16 paternal) were inherited from unaffected or pauci-symptomatic parents. Direct mapping to OMIM or Orphanet database entries was present in 22 patients (56.4%). The neurobehavioral phenotype was dominated by intellectual disability (ID)/developmental delay (DD) (26 patients, 66.7%), dysmorphic features (18 patients, 46.2%) and autism spectrum disorder (ASD) (15 patients, 38.5%), followed by developmental coordination disorder (10 patients, 25.6%), Specific Language Disorder/Communication Disorder (SLD) (10 patients, 25.6%), Disruptive behavioral disorders (7 patients, 17.9%), ADHD (4 patients, 10.3%), microcephaly (3 patients, 7.7%), structural brain MRI abnormalities (3 patients, 7.7%), epilepsy (3 patients, 7.7%) EEG abnormalities (2 patients, 5.1%) and selective mutism (2 patients, 5.1%). The cumulative clinical burden ranged from 1 to 6 manifestations per patient (median: 2, IQR: 2-3), with 82.1% of patients presenting with 2-3 co-occurring features. Conclusions: The identification of CNVs syndromes and associated clinical phenotypes is of significant support in the diagnostic process and possible therapeutic management. ID and ASD represent the core diagnostic drivers, while the high rate of inherited CNVs and multi-domain comorbidity underscore the impact of variable expressivity and cumulative clinical burden in neurodevelopmental disorders.

items.title: Effects of Non-Pharmacological Interventions on Theory of Mind in Older Adults: A Systematic Literature Review.
items.authors: Ferreira DA, Osório FL.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Aging is associated with declines in processing speed, executive functioning, and Theory of Mind (ToM), which may compromise social functioning. ToM interventions, developed mainly for autism and schizophrenia, have been tested in older adults, but their effects remain unsynthesized. This systematic review synthesized the effects of non-pharmacological interventions on ToM in healthy older adults and in those with neurodegenerative/neurocognitive disorders. Methods: Following PRISMA 2020, PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, Scopus, and PsycINFO were searched from inception to 25 January 2026, without language restrictions. Studies reporting at least one performance-based ToM outcome pre/post intervention were eligible. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data; methodological quality was appraised with the Effective Public Health Practice Project (EPHPP) tool, and findings were synthesized narratively by intervention category. Results: Seventeen studies (19 interventions; n = 762; mean age 69.6 years; 73.6% healthy) were included. Eleven interventions were ToM-targeted and eight non-ToM-targeted. ToM improved in 10 of 11 ToM-targeted interventions (91%) at immediate post-intervention, with predominantly moderate-to-large effects; non-ToM-targeted interventions yielded selective gains, mainly in cognitive rather than affective ToM. Nine studies (53%) had weak methodological quality; follow-up was scarce and short, and 88% of the evidence originated in Europe. Conclusions: ToM-targeted interventions in older adults appear promising, although no single intervention is clearly superior. The diversity of strategies, which operate through partially distinct mechanisms, hinders direct comparison but may broaden applicability across clinical profiles and care settings. Evidence remains limited by methodological weaknesses, predominantly healthy samples with preserved baseline cognition, heterogeneous ToM measures, scarce follow-up, and geographic concentration. Future trials should enroll clinical samples and use standardized ToM outcomes.

items.title: Genetic Variation Shapes MECP2-Dependent Vulnerability to Stress-Related Adverse Mental Health Trajectories in Women.
items.authors: Cosentino L, Cardillo V, Nisticò L, De Filippis B, Fagnani C, Medda E.

sections.text: The multi-factorial origin of stress vulnerability remains incompletely understood, hampering the implementation of targeted prevention. As interplays between genes and environment lie at the basis of individual variability, epigenetic mechanisms are considered important mediators of adverse mental health trajectories following stressful experiences. We have previously demonstrated that the X-linked epigenetic factor Methyl-CpG binding protein 2 (MECP2) plays a role in stress susceptibility, with dysfunctional variants in transgenic mice and its downregulation in human populations being associated with a lower ability to cope with adverse events. By leveraging a study of the Italian Twin Registry on mental health during the COVID-19 pandemic, the present study explored whether a genetic component that accounts for individual variability in MECP2 expression may shape risk of developing stress-related mental health deterioration. We report an association between homozygosity for the minor allele of the rs2734647, a single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) in the MECP2 3'-untranslated region (UTR) that has been linked to allele-specific MECP2 downregulation, and increased symptoms of COVID-19 pandemic-related depression, anxiety and distress in women. Our findings provide additional evidence for the emerging role of MECP2 in stress vulnerability, unveiling the contribution of genetic variation within the MECP2 locus to adverse mental health outcomes in women.

items.title: Genetic mechanisms underlying the associations between brain structure and mental health.
items.authors: Hu K, Tian X, Lou J, Ding C, Zhang T, Zhang H, Zhang X, Liu B.

sections.text: Brain-wide association studies have linked brain structure to complex mental health phenotypes, yet the genetic underpinnings of these effects remain largely unclear. Here, we leverage multimodal neuroimaging, behavioral and genetic data from the UK Biobank to develop an integrative framework combining brain-wide association studies and GWAS to elucidate how genetic variants affect the relationship between brain structure and mental health. Our multivariate brain-wide association study identifies two reproducible brain structural modes: a cerebellar-dominant mode and a cortical-dominant mode that explain individual differences in mental health measures. Using GWAS, we subsequently identify 30 and 15 independent significant variants respectively for each mode, indicating distinct genetic architectures with no signal overlap. Post-GWAS analyses indicate distinct biological pathways: the cerebellar-dominant mode is enriched for genes involved in chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation, while the cortical-dominant mode is linked to neurotransmitter metabolism. Moreover, we identify shared genetic influences between the brain modes and both mental health and cognitive traits, as well as causal effects of the brain modes on these outcomes. We validate the framework in the independent HCP cohort, supporting the cross-cohort generalizability of the identified brain-behavior and genetic associations.

items.title: Associations Between Chronic Diarrhea and Geriatric Syndromes, Dietary Habits, and Health Outcomes Among Community-Dwelling Older Adults.
items.authors: Marzetti E, Coelho-Júnior HJ.

sections.text: Background: The present study examined the associations between chronic diarrhea and geriatric syndromes, dietary habits, and health outcomes among community-dwelling older adults. Methods: This cross-sectional study included data from the 2005-2006, 2007-2008, and 2009-2010 NHANES cycles. The primary analytical sample comprised 3498 adults aged ≥65 years with available information on chronic diarrhea. Chronic diarrhea was operationalized according to participants usual stool consistency using the Bristol Stool Form Scale (types 6-7). Outcomes included disability, multimorbidity, polypharmacy, frailty, risk of sarcopenia, malnutrition, sleep disorders, dietary patterns, self-rated diet quality, hospital admission, and mental health service use. Logistic and linear regression models were used to examine associations, with adjusted models including age and sex. The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was applied to control the false discovery rate (FDR). Results: Chronic diarrhea was identified in 328 participants (9.4%). After adjustment for age and sex, chronic diarrhea was associated with higher odds of disability in basic (OR 1.69, 95% CI 1.15-2.48) and instrumental activities of daily living (OR 1.78, 95% CI 1.37-2.31), polypharmacy (OR 1.42, 95% CI 1.13-1.78), and frailty (OR 2.26, 95% CI 1.26-4.02). Participants with chronic diarrhea were also less likely to report good dietary quality (OR 0.55, 95% CI 0.42-0.72). These five associations remained statistically significant after FDR correction (q < 0.05). Although chronic diarrhea was initially associated with sleep disorders (OR 1.89, 95% CI 1.08-3.30), this association did not remain significant after FDR correction (q = 0.121). No significant associations were observed with multimorbidity, sarcopenia-related measures, malnutrition, protein or fiber intake, dietary-pattern scores, hospital admission, or mental health service use. Conclusions: These findings suggest that usual loose or watery stools may identify older adults with greater functional and clinical vulnerability. However, the results should be interpreted cautiously, and longitudinal studies incorporating the NHANES sampling design and more comprehensive confounder adjustment are needed.
