items.title: Affiliate stigma is associated with caregiver burden through reduced self-efficacy among caregivers of preschool children with autism spectrum disorder: a moderated mediation study.
items.authors: Chai R, Dong Y, Li Y, Chai R.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: Family caregivers of children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD) are vulnerable to affiliate stigma and caregiver burden, yet the psychological pathway linking stigma to burden and the family-level conditions that may buffer this pathway remain insufficiently understood. This study examined whether self-efficacy mediated the association between affiliate stigma and caregiver burden and whether caregiver support availability moderated this indirect association.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: In this cross-sectional study, 456 primary family caregivers of children aged 3-7 years with ASD were recruited from tertiary hospitals in Shandong Province, China. Participants completed the Zarit Burden Interview, General Self-Efficacy Scale, Affiliate Stigma Scale, and a demographic and caregiving questionnaire. Correlation analysis, hierarchical regression, bootstrap mediation analysis, and conditional process analysis were performed.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Affiliate stigma was positively correlated with caregiver burden (ρ = 0.28, p  < 0.001) and negatively correlated with self-efficacy (ρ = -0.16, p  < 0.001). Self-efficacy partially mediated the association between affiliate stigma and caregiver burden, accounting for 12.6% of the total effect (indirect effect = 0.031, 95% CI: 0.011-0.057). Caregiver support availability moderated the mediated pathway. The indirect effect was significant among caregivers with low support availability (effect = 0.044, 95% CI: 0.018-0.078) but not among those with high support availability (effect = 0.003, 95% CI: -0.029 to 0.033).

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: Affiliate stigma was associated with greater caregiver burden partly through lower self-efficacy, while higher co-caregiving support availability was associated with an attenuated indirect association. Stigma reduction, self-efficacy enhancement, and family support mobilization should be integrated into mental health support for caregivers of preschool children with ASD.

items.title: Beyond monotherapy: sex- and age-stratified pharmacovigilance of blonanserin adverse events focusing on drug-drug interactions.
items.authors: Zeng S, Chen S, Shang D, Wang Z.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: Blonanserin is an atypical antipsychotic that has been marketed in several Asian countries, but the drug-drug interaction (DDI) signals between it and commonly co-prescribed medications have not been systematically evaluated.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This study aimed to systematically explore adverse event (AE) signals for blonanserin both as monotherapy and in combination therapies, using the Japanese Adverse Drug Event Report (JADER) database.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: For monotherapy, disproportionality analysis (Reporting Odds Ratio, Proportional Reporting Ratio, Bayesian Confidence Propagation Neural Network) was used to detect potential signals. Time-to-onset (TTO) analysis was further applied to monotherapy signals using the Weibull distribution and group distribution analyses. For DDI assessment, five disproportionality methods were employed (Ω shrinkage, additive, multiplicative, combination risk ratio, and chi-square statistics model). Subgroup analyses were stratified by sex and age. Firth's penalized logistic regression was performed for DDI signals, adjusting for sex and age. Two sensitivity analyses were conducted.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Monotherapy analysis identified 87 positive AE signals for blonanserin, including rhabdomyolysis, neuroleptic malignant syndrome, falls, and sedation complications. TTO analysis suggested an early-onset pattern for the reported AEs. DDI analysis identified 268 positive drug-drug-AE disproportionality signals, predominantly involving combinations with benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, and antiepileptics. The strongest disproportionality DDI signals were blonanserin + noradrenaline (n = 10, Ω_0.25 = 3.12, AE = drug interaction). The most frequently observed DDI signals involved blonanserin + estazolam (n = 18, Ω_0.25 = 1.50, AE = rhabdomyolysis). Subgroup analyses revealed significant differences in DDI reporting signals between sexes and between patients aged <60 and ≥60 years. Regression analyses showed that 97.01% of the identified DDI signals remained statistically significant, even after adjusting for sex and age. Sex and age were independently associated with the reporting of specific DDI signals. Both sensitivity analyses indicated that 81.54% of the DDI signals were robust across both scenarios.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: This study identified potential safety signals associated with the concomitant use of blonanserin, particularly when used in combination with benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, and antiepileptic drugs. Sex- and age-related differences were observed in the reporting patterns of specific DDI signals, suggesting that demographic factors may warrant consideration when monitoring the safety of blonanserin combination therapies. Given the inherent limitations of spontaneous reporting databases, further pharmacoepidemiological studies are warranted to validate these signals and investigate potential causality.

items.title: Blood and urine metabolomics in children with autism spectrum disorder: biomarker discovery and clinical translation within a multi-pathway convergence framework.
items.authors: Guo F, Zhang Y, Kong Y, Ma B.

sections.text: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) is a neurodevelopmental condition characterized by deficits in social communication and restricted, repetitive behaviors, and is diagnosed in an increasing proportion of children worldwide. Diagnosis is currently based on standardized behavioral observation and developmental history, and no validated biological marker is yet available for routine clinical use. Metabolomics, a key branch of systems biology, captures the downstream metabolic phenotype resulting from gene-environment interactions, offering a complementary avenue for identifying candidate biomarkers and elucidating mechanisms in ASD. In recent years, blood- and urine-based metabolomic studies have identified alterations across several metabolic domains in children with ASD-amino acid and lipid metabolism, oxidative stress and antioxidant defense, gut-microbiota-derived metabolites, mitochondrial/energy metabolism, and purine metabolism. Nevertheless, cross-study consistency of reported biomarkers remains limited, and methodological challenges-including small sample sizes, analytical platform heterogeneity, and inadequate control of confounding factors-constrain the translation of research findings into clinical diagnostic tools. This narrative review integrates the latest evidence from blood and urine metabolomics within a "multi-pathway convergence" framework, constructing a six-domain panoramic map of metabolic disturbances in children with ASD, evaluating the complementarity and convergent value of dual-biofluid biomarkers, delineating the metabolic features with the most reproducible cross-biofluid patterns, and proposing a phased translational pathway from biomarker discovery to clinical diagnostic panel development.

items.title: Longitudinal interaction between emotional regulation difficulties and psychological distress in stroke patients and their spouses during rehabilitation and nursing implications.
items.authors: Li F, Mao Y, Huang C.

sections.heading: Objective
sections.text: This longitudinal study examined the dynamic interaction between emotion regulation difficulties and psychological distress in stroke rehabilitation patients and their spouses using the Actor-Partner Interdependence Model (APIM).

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Between June 2023 and June 2025, 394 patient-spouse dyads were recruited from the Department of Rehabilitation Medicine at Shaoxing People's Hospital using cluster sampling. A six-month longitudinal investigation was conducted across three phases: pre-rehabilitation (T1), early rehabilitation (T2), and rehabilitation maintenance (T3). The Difficulties in Emotion Regulation Scale and Distress Thermometer were administered at each timepoint. Statistical analyses included measurement invariance testing and cross-lagged APIM analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Of 394 eligible couples, 386 completed all three surveys. Measurement invariance was established across timepoints (ΔCFI ≤ 0.01). Significant actor effects revealed bidirectional within-individual relationships: patients' and spouses' emotion dysregulation positively predicted their subsequent psychological distress (T1→T2: β = 0.19-0.21; T2→T3: β = 0.17-0.18; all p < 0.01). Conversely, psychological distress in both partners predicted later emotion dysregulation (T1→T2: β = 0.21-0.24, p < 0.001; T2→T3: β = 0.19-0.20, p < 0.01). Significant partner effects indicated inter-dyad transmission of psychological distress over time.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: These findings demonstrate reciprocal longitudinal associations between emotion dysregulation and psychological distress within individuals and between partners. Healthcare providers should prioritize simultaneous dyadic screening, and future studies should test whether family-centered interventions can interrupt these reciprocal patterns and reduce distress in both patients and caregivers.

items.title: Digital Parenting and Parent-Reported Internet Gaming Disorder-Related Symptoms Among Children: A Cross-Sectional Study.
items.authors: Saleh SR, AlBishi AN, Eltantawy MM.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Internet Gaming Disorder (IGD)-related symptoms are a concern for children's digital mental health, yet evidence on digital parenting as a family-context correlate of these symptoms is limited. This study examined the concurrent associations of total digital parenting and its two operational dimensions, Digital Knowledge and Technical Competence (DKTC) and Digital Guidance, Protection, and Engagement (DGPE), with parent-reported IGD-related symptom severity.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This cross-sectional survey included 285 parent reports from Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, each concerning one child aged 6-13 years ( M = 8.76, SD = 1.32; 55.4% boys). Parents completed an adapted parent-report IGDS9-SF and a 15-item digital-parenting scale. Correlations and hierarchical regression with HC3 standard errors and bootstrap intervals were used.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Symptom severity was inversely associated with total digital parenting ( r = -0.747), DKTC ( r = -0.658), and DGPE ( r = -0.710), all p < 0.001. The model containing the two dimensions accounted for 56.0% of the variance, nearly identical to the model containing the total score (55.9%); both dimensions showed unique inverse associations (β = -0.333 and -0.481, p < 0.001).

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Higher digital parenting was associated with lower parent-reported IGD-related symptom severity. Because the data were cross-sectional and reported by the same parent, causal or protective effects cannot be inferred.

items.title: Disability Certification Without Functional Assessment: Uneven Documentation Across Diagnostic Groups in Romania.
items.authors: Stănică MG, Popescu MN, Ursescu C, Săvulescu SE, Ciobanu I, Furtunescu FL, Popescu C, Berteanu M.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Disability certification in Romania rests mainly on medical diagnosis. We examined whether documented standardized functional assessment in certification dossiers differs across diagnostic groups. Methods: We analyzed 460 anonymized adult dossiers collected in January 2023, ten from each of 46 disability assessment commissions in 41 of Romania's 42 first-level administrative units. Because the commissions selected the files and at least half had to include a psychological evaluation, we compared diagnostic groups rather than estimating national rates and repeated the main comparison accounting for clustering. Results: Most files concerned older adults with neurocognitive or mental disorders; dementias accounted for 40.2% of primary diagnoses. An activity scale (ADL, IADL or Barthel Index) was documented in 69.0% of non-dementia neurological dossiers, 34.4% of dementia dossiers and 10.8% of other mental-disorder dossiers; the gradient persisted after accounting for clustering. Cognitive and global instruments were documented more often than activity scales. Conclusions: Functional evidence was scarcest in neurocognitive and mental disorders, in which diagnosis predicts functioning least well. The national criteria list activity scales for neurological conditions but only cognitive and global instruments for neurocognitive and mental disorders; adding activity scales for these groups, then ICF-based assessment such as WHODAS 2.0, would address the gap.

items.title: Heterogeneity of Medical Students' Perceived Involution and Its Associated Factors: A Latent Profile Analysis.
items.authors: Song Y, Zhu L, Huang X, Li J, Liang H, Luo A, Liang Y, Yang Y.

sections.text: Objectives: This study aimed to identify latent profiles of perceived involution among medical students and examine their associated demographic and psychological factors. Methods: From March to July 2026, 499 medical students were recruited through convenience sampling at Guangdong Pharmaceutical University, China. Participants completed a demographic questionnaire and measures of perceived involution, academic involution climate, self-concept clarity, and perceived stress. Latent profile analysis was performed using the 18 perceived involution items, followed by R3STEP multinomial logistic regression to examine factors associated with profile membership. Results: Three perceived in-volution profiles were identified: low (25.7%), medium (46.9%), and high (27.5%), with an entropy of 0.872. Academic involution climate, self-concept clarity, and perceived stress scores differed significantly across the three profiles ( p < 0.05). Multinomial logistic regression showed that only-child status, a stronger academic involution climate, and higher perceived stress were associated with greater odds of being classified into the high perceived involution group rather than the low or medium group. Conclusions: Perceived involution among medical students exhibited heterogeneity, with the medium profile accounting for the largest proportion. Academic involution climate, perceived stress, and family characteristics were associated with classification into different perceived involution groups. These findings provide a reference for understanding differences in medical students' perceived involution and developing appropriate student support strategies.

items.title: Protocol for a Randomized Controlled Trial of a Clinician-Supervised Home-School-Hospital-Linked Digital-Health-Platform-Supported Conservative Management Pathway for Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis.
items.authors: Zeng Q, Yue Z, Zhang L, Li X, Hu R.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) brings substantial physical and psychological burden for affected teenagers. Current conservative follow-up management is fragmented under routine clinical settings. This study aims to assess the effectiveness of a multimodal health-management-platform-assisted care pathway for adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis receiving conservative treatment. Methods: This is a single-center, superiority, parallel-group, 1:1 randomized controlled trial with assessor-blinded outcome evaluation. A total of 76 eligible adolescent participants will be randomly allocated into either the control group receiving routine guideline-based conservative care or the intervention group receiving clinician-supervised platform-supported collaborative care. Participants will complete assessments at baseline and at 4 months (primary endpoint), 8 months, and 12 months of follow-up. The primary outcome is the change in Cobb angle from baseline to 4 months. Secondary outcomes include treatment adherence, mental health status, medical expenditure, participant and guardian satisfaction, and safety outcomes. The primary analysis will follow the intention-to-treat principle. This manuscript describes the trial protocol. The first participant was enrolled on 26 March 2025; to date, 35 out of the target 76 participants have been recruited. No primary endpoint outcome data have been unlocked or analyzed at the time of this protocol version. Conclusions: This trial will evaluate whether a clinician-supervised, platform-supported collaborative care pathway improves Cobb-angle outcomes and care-process measures compared with routine guideline-based conservative care in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis. This trial will generate comparative evidence regarding clinical effectiveness and the care-process value of platform-supported collaborative care for conservatively managed AIS adolescents.

Participants will complete assessments at baseline and at 4 months (primary endpoint), 8 months, and 12 months of follow-up. The primary outcome is the change in Cobb angle from baseline to 4 months. Secondary outcomes include treatment adherence, mental health status, medical expenditure, participant and guardian satisfaction, and safety outcomes. The primary analysis will follow the intention-to-treat principle. This manuscript describes the trial protocol. The first participant was enrolled on 26 March 2025; to date, 35 out of the target 76 participants have been recruited. No primary endpoint outcome data have been unlocked or analyzed at the time of this protocol version. Conclusions: This trial will evaluate whether a clinician-supervised, platform-supported collaborative care pathway improves Cobb-angle outcomes and care-process measures compared with routine guideline-based conservative care in adolescents with idiopathic scoliosis. This trial will generate comparative evidence regarding clinical effectiveness and the care-process value of platform-supported collaborative care for conservatively managed AIS adolescents.

items.title: Regional Disparities in Registered Autism Spectrum Disorder Cases and Child Psychiatry Workforce Capacity in Kazakhstan, 2015-2025: A Nationwide Registry-Based Study.
items.authors: Mansharipova Z, Turgambayeva A, Toktabayeva B, Abylgazinova A, Kapanova G, Temirkhanova R, Imanmadiyeva D, Dauletyarova M, Utegenova A, Mussakhanova A.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Newly registered autism spectrum disorder (ASD) cases in Kazakhstan have increased, but population-standardized regional variation and its relation to child psychiatry workforce capacity have not been described.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This retrospective ecological study used annual psychiatric service reports (Form 10-f, Ministry of Health) for 2015-2025, including newly registered cases coded F84.0, F84.1 and F84.5 among children aged 0-17 years. Rates per 100,000 children were calculated nationally and for 16 historical-boundary regions. The national trend was modeled using negative binomial regression and regional inequality using the Gini coefficient.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The national rate of newly registered ASD cases increased from 3.9 to 63.5 per 100,000 children (average annual rate ratio 1.32, 95% CI 1.31-1.34), whereas child psychiatrist density declined from 2.06 to 1.43 per 100,000 children and the ratio of newly registered cases to child psychiatrists increased from 1.9 to 44.3. In 2025, regional rates ranged from 28.7 to 221.4 (Astana) per 100,000 children. The Gini coefficient of regional rates decreased from 0.64 to 0.32.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Registered ASD cases increased markedly while child psychiatrist density declined, and registration rates varied substantially between regions. These data describe registration rather than prevalence, and regional estimates are subject to uncertainty in population denominators.

items.title: Support Needs, Care Gaps and Preferences Across the Paediatric Congenital Heart Surgery Care Continuum: A Scoping Review Based Primarily on Parent and Caregiver Reports.
items.authors: Petsios K, Drakouli M, Dousis E, Albani E.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Congenital heart surgery combines episodes of critical illness with continuing family caregiving. This scoping review mapped child- and parent-reported support needs, preferences and care gaps across the surgical continuum and identified implications for family-centred nursing care. Methods: Following JBI guidance and PRISMA-ScR, PubMed, CINAHL Complete and Scopus scientific databases were searched to identify English-language primary evidence published between January 2010 and July 2026. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts and assessed the original full texts; both confirmed the eligibility of four revision-stage additions. Descriptive mapping and content analysis classified reports by care stage, support domain and reporter. Results: The findings primarily reflect parent and caregiver accounts of support needs, care gaps and preferences across the surgical continuum. Database searching yielded 2263 records. Following record reconciliation and reference checking, 154 reports were assessed, with 73 included in the study. Information or education was represented in 55 reports (75.3%), followed by emotional or psycho-social support (43, 58.9%), communication or participation (40, 54.8%), and discharge or home-care support (32, 43.8%). Discharge, home and interstage care was the care stage grouping most represented (21, 28.8%). Five reports (6.8%) included the perspectives of children and adolescents alongside caregivers. The limited inclusion of child and adolescent perspectives restricts conclusions about children's own priorities and highlights the need for developmentally appropriate research that elicits their views directly. Conclusions: The review provides a stage-specific map linking reported support requirements to potential nursing responses. Priorities include repeated needs assessment, tailored communication, family participation, discharge preparation and coordinated support. These responses require evaluation, while the limited representation of children's perspectives restricts conclusions about their own priorities.

items.title: "I Don't Trust It, but I Have to Trust It": Trust vs. Use of Online Technology Across the Mental Health Spectrum in the UK.
items.authors: Palmer-Cooper EC, Gentry E, Nichele E, Azim T, Naiseh M, Dowthwaite L, Armouch MS, Greenway F, Weal M, Hughes AM.

sections.text: Use of internet-based technologies (IBTs) and artificial intelligence (AI) via eHealth could enhance mental healthcare delivery and accessibility. However, ethical concerns, perceptions of AI capabilities, past experience, and individual differences can influence acceptance and engagement. We qualitatively explored attitudes and behaviours toward IBTs, AI and eHealth, given the overlapping nature of these digital environments, trust, and the possible role of mental health. This exploratory study conducted semi-structured interviews between March and October 2023 with 22 UK-based participants: eight with lived experience of a mental health problem and 14 without. There was no clear difference in participants' levels of trust in IBTs across mental health status. Participants reported using IBTs despite privacy concerns. Trust was influenced by perceptions of developer trustworthiness, individual traits, and affective responses to IBTs. Convenience, ease of use, and lack of alternatives often outweighed concerns, driving engagement. Our findings highlight that in this group trust is a key factor in IBT and eHealth uptake, but not the sole determinant, highlighting ethical concerns and responsibilities for both UK healthcare providers and developers. There is a need for transparent, ethically grounded, value-sensitive design and implementation of IBTs and AI-enabled eHealth tools that supports genuine user choice, voluntary engagement, and human interaction.

items.title: Beyond Stress Buffering: An Interactional Stigma Amplification Pattern Linking COVID-19 Discrimination Experiences and Mental Health Among COVID-19 Survivors.
items.authors: Xu T, Liao T, Zhou S.

sections.text: Social interaction is generally regarded as a protective resource for mental health; however, its role may be more complex in contexts characterized by stigma and discrimination. This study examined the association between COVID-19-related discrimination experiences and mental health among people with a history of COVID-19 infection, focusing on the moderating role of social interaction continuity. Using survey data from 1248 respondents with a history of COVID-19 infection, we measured COVID-19-related discrimination experiences based on seven types of discrimination or social exclusion, social interaction continuity using three items assessing changes in social interaction, and mental health using a nine-item scale. Ordinary least squares regression models were used to examine these associations and the interaction between discrimination experiences and social interaction continuity, adjusting for demographic and socioeconomic characteristics and social support. The results showed that greater exposure to COVID-19-related discrimination was associated with poorer mental health. Social interaction continuity was positively associated with mental health, consistent with traditional stress-buffering perspectives. Moreover, the interaction between discrimination experiences and social interaction continuity was negative and marginally significant (β = -0.0767, p < 0.1). Conditional-effect analyses suggested that the negative association between discrimination experiences and mental health was stronger at higher levels of social interaction continuity. These findings provide preliminary evidence of an interactional pattern consistent with stigma amplification, suggesting that social interaction may serve both as a source of psychosocial support and as a context for stigma-related social evaluation and stress.

items.title: Chinese Master's Students' Emerging Understandings of Group Work in Experiential Training: A Process-Relational Perspective.
items.authors: Xiao J, Xiang X.

sections.text: Competency frameworks specify what effective group work requires, but less is known about how beginners develop an understanding of group work. This qualitative study examined how students with limited prior group counseling experience understood group work during a five-week experiential component of a group counseling course in a Chinese master's-level Mental Health Education program. Using reflexive thematic analysis, we examined 536 weekly reflective journals from 108 students, including comparisons of individual participants' reflections across the five weeks. Three interconnected themes were developed: learning to see the group as a structured, developing relational whole; learning to facilitate through purposeful design, the fostering of member-to-member interaction, and attention to the relational consequences of facilitation choices; and positioning the self through revised self-appraisal, awareness of influence, and emerging professional orientation. Students connected these understandings with participation in a continuing peer group, rotating facilitation roles, and opportunities to revisit experiences through reflective writing and instructor-guided review. Taken together, the findings point to an emerging process-relational perspective on group work, in which facilitation skills are considered in relation to how actions shape group processes and members' opportunities to participate. The study adds group-specific detail to accounts of early professional learning, while recognizing that reflective journals capture emerging understandings rather than demonstrate stable behavioral competence.

items.title: Coping with Poor Sleep at University: A Qualitative Study of Student Perspectives and Implications for Personalised Interventions.
items.authors: Riazi A, Carboni T, Miranda F.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Although it has been established that poor sleep is common in university students, there is some evidence that this has worsened in the post-pandemic era, where irregular sleep patterns and reliance on technology became widespread in young people. This qualitative study explored the experiences of young people who were experiencing poor sleep.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: Using purposive sampling, 13 undergraduate students reporting sleep difficulties were recruited from academic institutions in the UK, Italy, and Portugal. In-depth interviews were conducted between July 2022 and January 2023, and data were analysed using thematic analysis.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Four themes were constructed: (I) Feeling unable to shake off the lingering effects of COVID lockdown, (II) Hypnotic effects of smartphone usage, (III) Being stuck in a loop of poor sleep and low mood, and (IV) Desperately trying to regain control over sleep. Students were eager to remedy their lack of sleep, but some behaviours, such as excessive social media use and late-night rumination contributed to a vicious cycle of negative emotions further disrupting their sleep, which in turn, worsened these feelings. The normalisation of some sleep-related behaviours among young people contributed to their maintenance.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: In order to develop effective sleep interventions, it is important to recognise the complex and interconnected factors associated with poor sleep in this population. The findings may inform the development of personalised, targeted interventions that address both the psychological and behavioural factors associated with sleep difficulties in university students.

items.title: Institutional Support and Betrayal Among LGBQ+ Student Survivors of Sexual Violence: College Students' Expectations and Experiences with Institutional Handling of Sexual Misconduct.
items.authors: Poole NQ, Amaya S, Hoogerwerf R, Gray MJ.

sections.text: Institutional betrayal (IB) occurs when an organization violates the trust of its constituents by failing to prevent or sufficiently respond to acts of harm This act of betrayal is especially common amongst victim-survivors of sexual violence. Considering higher rates of victimization among LGBQ+ individuals, this population may be at greater risk of experiencing IB and related negative outcomes). The current study intends to expand understanding of student perceptions of institutional responding to sexual violence across sexual orientation. The present investigation compared IB and institutional support (IS) among heterosexual and LGBQ+ students as well as victim-survivors' subsequent mental health and functional outcomes. Results were obtained from 1913 university students using a large sexual misconduct campus climate survey. LGBQ+ students experienced sexual assault at higher rates and reported poorer appraisals of campus climate, safety, and institutional responding. Interaction effects suggest that victim-survivors reported more IB than non-victim-survivors, though this did not differ as a function of orientation. However, non-victim-survivors' expectations of IB did differ as a function of orientation, with LGBQ+ individuals expecting more IB. Victim-survivors who disclosed to university-affiliated sources endorsed significantly less IB than those who did not. Formal reporting among LGBQ+ victim-survivors was associated with poorer mental health outcomes but reduced dissatisfaction with their institution, the latter of which evidenced an opposite pattern for heterosexual victim-survivors. These results provide a novel contribution to the current understanding of IB amongst LGBT+ survivors and may be relevant for university efforts to support LGBQ+ student survivors.

items.title: Prioritizing Research Team Infrastructure and Well-Being: Structural Healing in a CBPR Mental Health Intervention Study with Latine Newcomers.
items.authors: Vasquez Guzman CE, Echeverri Herrera S, Hess JM, Galvis M, Casas N, Medina Bustillos DA, Ramirez JD, Ramirez S, Aguirre I, Parker D, Medina M, Mendoza A, Placios V, Goodkind JR.

sections.text: Community-based participatory research (CBPR) offers a transformative framework for designing and implementing mental health interventions among newcomers, particularly forcibly displaced people with compounding stressors. However, maintaining meaningful participatory processes during the implementation phase of intervention studies is challenging. As part of the praxis of the Immigrant Well-being Project (IWP), a study that involved adapting and implementing an evidence-based mental health intervention for Latine newcomers, the community-university research team took detailed notes at research team meetings and retreats, maintained a decision log, and engaged in ongoing critical reflection and discussion on CBPR processes from 2017 to 2023. Through critical reflective analysis, we identified three participatory priorities: (1) maintaining flexibility and responsive research team infrastructure; (2) addressing emergent structural constraints; and (3) centering individual and collective well-being as dynamic practices. We also identified multiple practices that enabled the team to maintain each priority, as well as the impacts these priorities and practices had on research team members. By attending to these structural conditions and the well-being of research team members, a form of structural healing was enacted to redistribute epistemic power and affirm the dignity of community members historically marginalized within healthcare and research settings.

items.title: Psychological Distress Among Oncology Nurses and Their Attitudes Toward Seeking Professional Psychological Help.
items.authors: Andargeery SY, Alenazi DF, AlOthman NO, Al Mutairi RA, AlShahrani RA, Alqahtani SA, Aldhafeeri NS, Alshomrani RM, Alwesmi MB.

sections.text: Oncology nursing is emotionally demanding and may place nurses at risk of psychological distress. However, distress does not necessarily translate into willingness to seek professional psychological support. This study aimed to assess psychological distress among oncology and non-oncology nurses and examine their attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help. A cross-sectional study was conducted among 155 registered nurses at a single government hospital in Riyadh. Psychological distress was assessed using the 10-item Kessler Psychological Distress Scale (K10), while attitudes toward professional psychological help were measured using the Attitudes Toward Seeking Professional Psychological Help Scale-Short Form (ATSPPH-SF). Descriptive and inferential statistical analyses were performed to compare oncology and non-oncology nurses and examine the association between psychological distress and help-seeking attitudes. Overall, nurses reported moderate psychological distress, with severe distress reported by a substantial proportion of participants. The distribution of psychological distress categories did not differ between oncology and non-oncology nurses (χ^2(3) = 2.01, p = 0.571). Attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help were generally close to the scale midpoint. These attitudes did not differ significantly between oncology and non-oncology nurses (U = 2771.5, p = 0.434) or across psychological distress categories (χ^2(3) = 4.538, p = 0.209). Psychological distress is a substantial concern among nurses, across both oncology and non-oncology departments. However, no statistically significant association was identified between the level of psychological distress and attitudes toward seeking professional psychological help. Healthcare organizations should implement proactive, confidential, and accessible mental health support strategies and promote a workplace culture that normalizes professional psychological help-seeking among nurses.

items.title: Stress, Vulnerability and Protection in Mental Health Risk Among Chinese University Students: A Grounded Theory Study.
items.authors: Wang F, Zheng F, Guo J, Yang G.

sections.text: Many correlates of poor mental health at university are known, but not why students in the same cohort fare so differently. This study aimed to derive a testable account of how mental health risk forms among university students. A grounded theory study combining Strauss-Corbin coding procedures with a constructivist stance was conducted at three universities in China in 2025. Forty participants (19 students, 14 school psychological counsellors and 7 student affairs counsellors) were interviewed in Mandarin (1253 min), and transcripts were coded at open, axial and selective levels in NVivo 12. Rigour was supported by triangulation, double-coding, member checking and negative case analysis. Coding yielded 82 initial categories, consolidated into 14 subcategories under three main categories: environmental stressors (S), vulnerability traits (V) and protective factors (P); 72.0% of categories were raised by all three informant groups. The core category was risk generation under stressor-vulnerability-protection interaction. Three contextual findings qualified existing frameworks: compressed microsystems, elements acting as both demand and resource, and a secondary pathway from impulsive conduct through institutional sanction to damaged standing. The resulting S-V-P model separates buffering of stress from compensation for vulnerability, distinguishes four levels of vulnerability, and places outcomes at both symptom and well-being poles. It is a context-specific, hypothesis-generating framework that awaits quantitative testing.

The core category was risk generation under stressor-vulnerability-protection interaction. Three contextual findings qualified existing frameworks: compressed microsystems, elements acting as both demand and resource, and a secondary pathway from impulsive conduct through institutional sanction to damaged standing. The resulting S-V-P model separates buffering of stress from compensation for vulnerability, distinguishes four levels of vulnerability, and places outcomes at both symptom and well-being poles. It is a context-specific, hypothesis-generating framework that awaits quantitative testing.

items.title: Will AI De-Skill Our Social Cognition? The Risks in the Delicate Interplay Between Artificial and Natural Theory of Mind.
items.authors: Pisauro MA, Fouragnan E.

sections.text: Theory of Mind (ToM) is a crucial component of human cognition and one of its distinguishing features. The development of Large Language Models capable of successfully performing ToM tests at levels similar or superior to those reached by humans has sparked a fierce debate and great interest in understanding how they do so. At the same time the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry is actively developing systems able to display human-like skills to better interact with humans. These systems routinely engage with millions of people, providing advice on interpersonal relations and mental health issues and serving as virtual companions in a myriad of roles. This process is driven by the developing ability to simulate interactions that reflect the social cognition processes that drive human behaviour, including ToM. Here we review the evidence and critically evaluate the concept of ToM in artificial and natural intelligence. We discuss the psychological and neural implications for human users interacting with an increasing number of "ToM-equipped" AI systems and potentially a decreasing number of other humans. We argue that, without strong regulations and societal education across the world, there is a real risk that AI will effectively de-skill human social cognition.

items.title: Natural Dopamine: Nature's Seven DIURNAL Environmental Enrichment Properties in Changing Visual Complexity.
items.authors: Khalil MH.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Time spent in unchanging environments is associated with poorer brain, cognitive and mental health outcomes, while environmental enrichment for humans is measured by how much nature is present rather than how it changes.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This study quantified nature's changing visual complexity using a large-language-model scoring method validated against a deep-learning complexity metric previously tested using event-related potentials. Photos were taken of a natural scene, a tree, and the sky across minutes, days, and seasons (1115 photographs; 2024 to 2026).

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: The analysis identified seven quantitative properties describing nature's dynamic environmental enrichment in changing visual complexity: Dichotomy, Inclination, Unpredictability, Renewal, Net balance, Amplitude, and Level (DIURNAL). A quantitative simulation then showed that a natural view offers more change than indoor and urban views, consistent with the argument that unchanging environments are detrimental to the brain, which is hypothesised here to act through a dopaminergic pathway.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: DIURNAL raises questions for biophilic design and for how neurotypical and neurodivergent brains respond to change in visual complexity in nature, digital environments and built environments.

items.title: Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation for Dysarthria in Parkinson's Disease: A Narrative Review.
items.authors: Luo X, Sun D, Li C, Li H, Tian L, Li X.

sections.text: Dysarthria is one of the common symptoms among patients with Parkinson's disease. It is mainly characterized by reduced volume, monotonous pitch, weakened stress, unstable speech rate, inaccurate pronunciation, and impaired rhythm, severely affecting the patients' quality of life and mental health. Numerous studies have indicated that the efficacy of pharmacotherapy and surgical therapy on articulation function remains inconsistent and controversial. In recent years, relevant studies have revealed that non-invasive brain stimulation can improve phonation in patients with Parkinson's disease, regulate the excitability of the stimulated brain regions and the functional connectivity between these regions and the cortices associated with speech control. However, existing research on non-invasive brain stimulation for the treatment of dysarthria in Parkinson's disease remains limited, characterized by inconsistent stimulation parameters, small sample sizes, and insufficient investigation into the underlying mechanisms. This narrative review summarizes the common techniques in non-invasive brain stimulation, including the research progress, potential mechanisms, and safety of repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation and transcranial direct current stimulation in the treatment of speech disorders in patients with Parkinson's disease. The aim is to further explore the feasibility of non-invasive brain stimulation in the treatment of dysarthria in Parkinson's disease, providing references and future directions for clinical practice.

items.title: Transcutaneous Auricular Vagus Nerve Stimulation in the Regulation of Brain Functional Homeostasis: A Literature Review.
items.authors: Bi H, Chen J, Li Y, Zhu Y.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Brain functional homeostasis encompasses coordinated electrophysiological, neuroimmune, neurovascular-metabolic, and neuroplastic regulatory processes, which may become perturbed in neurological and psychiatric disorders. Transcutaneous auricular vagus nerve stimulation (taVNS) provides a non-invasive approach to modulate this system. However, the interactions among these regulatory processes and their relationships with taVNS have not yet been comprehensively synthesized. This review asks what taVNS changes within each dimension and how directly the measurements reflect the process they are taken to represent.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: We searched PubMed (28 August 2026) and performed a complementary Web of Science search on 3 November 2026 for taVNS studies published between January 2016 and August 2026, using free-text terms for taVNS and its variants. After duplicate removal and title/abstract screening, records were assigned to clinical-evidence, mechanism-supplement, and reviews/meta-analyses libraries. Studies were eligible if they used taVNS at an explicit auricular site, addressed efficacy or mechanism, included an effect comparison, and reported a central or clinically relevant readout.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Evidence is unevenly distributed. Electrophysiological effects, including modulation of excitation/inhibition balance and oscillatory activity, have been documented directly in humans; neuroimmune effects rest largely on animal work on the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway and α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptor signaling; neurovascular and metabolic effects derive from a much smaller base; and neuroplastic effects are inferred mainly from molecular markers and imaging. Trials spanning major neurological, psychiatric, and perioperative indications report heterogeneous outcomes, and comparators are rarely physiologically inert.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Existing taVNS findings can be organized into four domains of brain functional homeostasis, although coordinated regulation across these domains and its contribution to clinical benefit remain to be established. Further progress requires well-controlled trials, standardized reporting of stimulation parameters and comparator conditions, validation of response biomarkers, and prospective evaluation of event-triggered stimulation.

items.title: Beyond emotional symptoms: multidomain routine outcome monitoring in psychiatric outpatient care
items.authors: Yu S, Luo H, Hu Z, Jiang X.

items.title: Cross-subject EEG emotion recognition network based on moment channel attention.
items.authors: Yang S, Han M.

sections.text: While most cross-subject EEG emotion recognition studies focus on average accuracy, the high inter-subject variability of EEG signals causes severe performance inconsistency across individuals. This inconsistency poses a critical barrier to real-world deployment but has received insufficient attention. To address this issue, this study proposes a hybrid emotion recognition model integrating moment channel attention and Transformer, termed the Moment Attention Convolution-Emotion Transformer Network (MAC-ETN). The proposed hybrid network consists of three components: a local temporal feature extractor, a Moment Channel Attention Network (MCA), and a global temporal feature extractor. Specifically, depthwise and separable convolutions are employed to extract local temporal features. The moment channel attention mechanism incorporates the first-order moment (mean), second-order moment (variance), and third-order moment (skewness) for channel importance calibration; and global dependency modeling is achieved through a Transformer encoder. Performance evaluation is conducted on two public datasets, DEAP and MAHNOB-HCI, using leave-one-subject-out cross-validation (LOSO-CV). The experimental results show that the main advantage of MAC-ETN lies in markedly reduced cross-subject performance variability rather than higher mean accuracy. On the DEAP dataset, the mean accuracy of MAC-ETN (61.26% for arousal and 60.47% for valence is lower than that of the strongest baselines reported under the same LOSO protocol, while its accuracy standard deviation (7.88% and 5.31%) is the lowest among all compared methods. On the MAHNOB-HCI dataset, the F1 standard deviation of MAC-ETN is 1.48% for arousal and 0.30% for valence, far below the values reported for the baselines in the literature, although the latter were obtained under a subject-dependent protocol and with a different F1 definition, so this comparison is indicative only. These results indicate that MAC-ETN reduces cross-subject performance variability at a moderate level of accuracy, which is relevant for practical EEG-based emotion recognition applications.

items.title: Exploring the association between heart rate variability and self-efficacy: A secondary analysis of a cross-sectional pilot study.
items.authors: Ho BYW, Ong E, Lam JYT, Hung WS, Wong BYM, Wong WK, Ng DTK, Liu TW, Law TY, Li Y, Tsang MY, Cheung ETY, Kwok CY.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: General self-efficacy (SE) may be associated with autonomic functioning, but evidence from healthy community samples remains limited. This exploratory study examined the cross-sectional associations between general SE and resting heart rate variability (HRV) and assessed whether SE explained HRV variance after adjustment for demographic characteristics.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: This secondary analysis used data from 97 healthy Chinese adults who participated in a cross-sectional pilot study. General SE was assessed using the Chinese General Self-Efficacy Scale, and resting HRV was recorded for five minutes using an ear-lobe photoplethysmography device. Spearman rank correlations were used to examine unadjusted associations between SE and 10 HRV indices, with false discovery rate correction for multiple comparisons. Principal component analysis was subsequently used to reduce redundancy among the HRV indices. Two-block hierarchical linear regression models examined whether SE explained incremental variance in the resulting HRV components after adjustment for age group and sex.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: In the unadjusted analyses, SE showed small inverse correlations with low-frequency power, SDNN, RMSSD, and mean inter-beat interval and a weak positive correlation with mean heart rate. Principal component analysis identified three components that collectively explained 84.9% of the variance in the HRV indices. After adjustment for age group and sex, SE did not explain a statistically significant increase in variance in any HRV component, contributing 0.3% to 2.4% of additional variance. Age group was significantly associated with two of the three components, whereas sex was not significantly associated with any component.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: Weak associations between SE and several resting HRV indices were observed in the unadjusted analyses, but these associations were attenuated in the covariate-adjusted component models. Demographic differences, particularly age, may partly account for the observed bivariate associations. Given the small convenience sample, cross-sectional design, and potential residual confounding, these findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger studies using physiological measurements.

items.title: Psychological safety and organizational silence in Turkish schools.
items.authors: Çakir S, Dagli G, Altinay Z, Altinay F, Yikici B.

sections.text: Organizational silence refers to employees intentionally withholding work-related ideas, concerns, or suggestions. This study examined psychological safety and organizational silence among 160 teachers and school administrators in public secondary schools in Türkiye. A correlational survey design was used. Psychological safety and organizational silence were measured with five-point Likert instruments, and the data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, group comparisons, Pearson correlation, and simple linear regression. Psychological safety was high (M = 3.58), whereas organizational silence was low (M = 2.47). The variables were moderately and negatively correlated (r = -.594, p <.001). Psychological safety accounted for 35.3% of the variance in organizational silence; because the design was cross-sectional, this finding indicates association rather than causation. No statistically significant differences were found by gender, position, age, professional seniority, or school type. The findings support school practices that reduce interpersonal risk and enable educators to raise questions and concerns.

items.title: Associations Between Physical Activity, Body Image Dissatisfaction, and Burnout Symptoms in Primary and Secondary School Teachers.
items.authors: Marconcin P, Santos V, Parreira M, Casanova N, Ramos P, Machado R, Serpa J.

sections.text: Background: Teaching is a high-demand profession associated with elevated levels of occupational stress and burnout. While physical activity and body image have been linked to psychological well-being, their independent and combined associations with burnout in teachers remain insufficiently understood, particularly regarding potential sex differences. Objectives: To examine the associations between physical activity, body image dissatisfaction, and burnout symptoms in teachers, and to determine whether these relationships differ between men and women. Methods: A cross-sectional secondary analysis was conducted using data from two independent datasets, comprising 189 teachers from primary and secondary education in the Setúbal district, Portugal. Burnout was assessed using the Maslach Burnout Inventory-Educators Survey (MBI-ES), body image was assessed using the Figure Rating Scale, and physical activity using the International Physical Activity Questionnaire-Short Form. Multiple linear and logistic regression analyses were performed, and moderation analyses were conducted, controlling for age and years of service. Results: Reporting any moderate-intensity physical activity was associated with higher personal accomplishment (β = 0.184, unadjusted p = 0.017), within a statistically significant overall regression model ( p = 0.015; Holm-adjusted p = 0.045). An exploratory association with lower depersonalization was also observed (β = -0.178, p = 0.024), although the overall regression model was not statistically significant ( p = 0.172). No significant association between physical activity and emotional exhaustion was observed. Absolute body image discrepancy showed an exploratory positive association with emotional exhaustion (β = 0.170, unadjusted p = 0.023), although the overall regression model was not statistically significant ( p = 0.088). No significant associations with depersonalization or personal accomplishment were observed. No statistically significant sex interactions were detected, although the moderation findings were inconclusive given the limited precision of the estimates. Conclusions: Reporting any moderate-intensity physical activity was associated with higher personal accomplishment in teachers, while its association with lower depersonalization should be interpreted as exploratory. Body image dissatisfaction, operationalized as absolute body image discrepancy, showed an exploratory association with emotional exhaustion, but no consistent associations were observed across burnout dimensions. These findings support a multidimensional perspective of teacher well-being and suggest that physical activity should be considered alongside occupational factors when investigating burnout in teachers. However, the cross-sectional design precludes conclusions regarding causal relationships.

items.title: LLM-Based AI Chatbot Use and Short-Term Issue-Specific Stress: The Role of Perceived Message Contingency.
items.authors: Kim H, Han JY, Zhang W, Yoon HJ, Seo JK.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: General-purpose large language model (LLM) chatbots are increasingly used to talk through everyday stressors, yet it is unclear whether a brief conversation with such a chatbot is followed by lower stress than consulting conventional online resources, and which perceived features of the exchange are associated with stress. Methods: In a randomized online experiment, 285 U.S. adults identified a personally relevant stressor and conversed with ChatGPT (GPT-3.5) or browsed non-conversational mental health websites for about 10 min. Issue-specific stress was assessed before and after the session. Results: Stress decreased in both conditions. Contrary to our hypothesis, post-session stress adjusted for pre-session stress did not differ between conditions (adjusted difference = 0.05, 95% CI [-0.16, 0.26]); an exploratory equivalence test supported equivalence within ±0.2 SD. ChatGPT use was associated with higher perceived message contingency, which was in turn associated with greater perceived social support of all four types. Perceived message contingency was associated with lower post-session stress (indirect effect = -0.15, 95% CI [-0.30, -0.01]), but this association was offset by a positive direct path; none of the hypothesized serial pathways through the four forms of support were clearly supported. Conclusions: A brief conversation with a general-purpose LLM chatbot was followed by post-session stress comparable to that after browsing reputable mental health websites and was experienced as more contingent and, for most forms of support, more supportive. Perceived contingency may be one feature linked to lower stress, but other features of the conversation appear to have worked in the opposite direction. The findings do not speak to clinical outcomes, sustained benefits, or the replacement of professional care.

items.title: Measuring the Mind Through the Body: A Critical Integrative Narrative Review of Stress and Psychological Inference in Consumer Wearables.
items.authors: Alves Ferreira JM, Giannouli V, Tragantzopoulou P.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Consumer wearables measure physiological and behavioural signals that may correlate with stress or affect, but physiological stress, subjective distress and psychiatric symptoms require different validation standards. This critical integrative narrative review examines which validation claims are supported and under which conditions. Methods: Structured literature searches were conducted from 9 April to 30 August 2026 in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, APA PsycINFO and IEEE Xplore, covering publications from January 2015 to 30 August 2026, with earlier foundational sources considered where pertinent. Recorded Boolean search strategies, narrative eligibility criteria and a descriptive evidence-appraisal framework guided a targeted integrative synthesis. As a narrative rather than systematic review, database hit counts and exclusion tallies were not recorded, and no PRISMA selection flow is asserted. items.title: Multidimensional Emotional Assessment for Community Mental Health: Exploring Sample-Based Reference Values for the Core Seven-Emotions Inventory-Short Form (CSEI-s).
items.authors: Cheong MJ, Kim J, Kang DH, Kook HJ, Jung IC, Lee DE, Kang HW.

sections.heading: Background/objectives
sections.text: Recognizing the types and intensity of everyday emotions helps people articulate distress and seek support. Community assessment therefore needs to describe coexisting emotions alongside specific symptoms. The Core Seven-Emotions Inventory-Short Form (CSEI-s), developed and initially validated in Korea, draws on traditional Korean medicine's Seven Emotions framework. However, references for interpreting scores across adult age groups remain limited. This study explored sample-based references for multidimensional emotional profiles.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: A cross-sectional online survey included 1769 adults aged 20-65 years recruited through non-probability sampling across 17 Korean regions. Subscale percentile ranks, linear T scores, and measurement-error estimates were derived. Internal consistency, factor structure, and demographic differences were examined.

sections.heading: Results
sections.text: Subscale Cronbach's α ranged from 0.736 to 0.900. A score of 12 corresponded to percentile ranks of 48.8 for Rumination/Pensiveness and 82.5 for Anger. Older groups generally reported lower scores. The correlated seven-factor model outperformed the alternatives without reaching adequate fit, and exploratory structural equation modeling revealed cross-loadings and poor separation of Fear from Fright.

sections.heading: Conclusions
sections.text: These preliminary references locate observed subscale scores within a defined sample. They are sample-based, non-diagnostic resources, not population norms or clinical thresholds, and individual interpretation awaits further validation.

items.title: Nurse Managers' Perspectives on Visit Cancellations in Psychiatric Home-Visit Nursing: A Qualitative Descriptive Study in Japan.
items.authors: Yayama S, Fujita S.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Visit cancellations in psychiatric home-visit nursing may be affected by service users' mental or physical conditions, daily circumstances, family involvement, relationships with staff, and service-delivery factors. Examining nurse managers' accounts of cancellation-related circumstances and reported responses may provide insights into care relationships and service delivery. This study aimed to identify factors perceived by nurse managers as contributing to visit cancellations, response strategies, and challenges and considerations involved in responding to cancellations in Japan. Methods: A qualitative descriptive study was conducted with eight nurse managers from independent psychiatric home-visit nursing stations in six Japanese prefectures. Individual semi-structured interviews were conducted in April-May 2024 and analyzed using a qualitative descriptive approach. Results: Six categories and 23 subcategories were identified across three domains: factors perceived as contributing to visit cancellations, response strategies, and challenges and considerations in responding to cancellations. Nurse managers identified service user- and family-related factors and service-related factors, including changes in mental or physical condition, schedule-management difficulties, limited perceived need for home-visit nursing, family involvement, staff approaches, service user-staff relationships, and discrepancies between expectations and received services. Responses included adjusting visit schedules, reconfirming the purpose of home-visit nursing, reviewing visit content and frequency, sharing cancellation information, reflecting on staff practices, and modifying staff assignments. Managers also described challenges related to unstable psychiatric symptoms, limited perceived need for home-visit nursing, and organizational reflection on cancellations. Conclusions: The findings suggest that responses to visit cancellations should consider service users' conditions and circumstances as well as care relationships, communication, family involvement, and service delivery. Understanding the circumstances underlying cancellations and adjusting support accordingly may provide opportunities to review care practices while respecting service users' preferences.

items.title: Resilience Buddy: A Multi-System Mobile Intervention for Mental Well-Being-Development and Pilot Evaluation.
items.authors: Fung KP, Wang Y, Kim S.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Digital interventions can promote mental health, and resilience is a key target for prevention. Resilience is often treated as an individual trait, overlooking the relational, material, and structural conditions that shape adaptation. The Multi-System Model of Resilience (MSMR) views resilience as a process that arises from three interacting systems (internal, intermediary, and external) across three levels of need (essential, situational, and actualization). This study describes the development of Resilience Buddy, a mobile intervention based on this model, and evaluates its usability, participant feedback on acceptability, and preliminary pre- to post-intervention changes in resilience and psychological distress. Methods: A single-arm formative pilot was conducted with adults who completed pre- and post-intervention assessments. The app includes 10 modules. The first is an introductory self-monitoring module, and the remaining nine are learning modules aligned with the model domains. Each learning module follows the same five-part sequence of values, inform & inspire, transcend, act, and link (VITAL). Outcomes were measured with the MSMR Inventory, the 12-item General Health Questionnaire, and the 4-item Usability Metric for User Experience. Data were analyzed with paired t tests, and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests were used as sensitivity analyses. Results: The analytic sample was 47 adults (mean age of 24.28 years, ranging from 19 to 45). Usability was moderate. Total resilience increased from pre to post (mean change of 7.23, p < 0.001), with the largest gains in the external-system domains. Psychological distress decreased (mean change -5.27, p < 0.001). Gains in resilience were associated with reductions in distress using Pearson's correlation, but not Spearman's. Conclusions: Resilience Buddy appears usable, acceptable, and associated with promising early improvements in resilience and distress. Controlled trials are needed to test efficacy and identify which domains respond most to digital intervention.

items.title: The Odds Are Fifty-Fifty: An Autoethnographic Account of Raising a Child with a Potential Adult-Onset Genetic Disease.
items.authors: Elmore C.

sections.heading: Background
sections.text: While knowledge is increasing about genetically inherited medical conditions, the personal accounts of parents faced with such unknowns for their child are rare. In this autoethnography, the author explores her years raising a daughter whose father was diagnosed with a previously unknown, incurable, autosomal dominant condition when the child was eleven. Because the condition is adult-onset, pediatricians and geneticists have long been advised to turn down parents' requests to have a minor child tested. The decision to test or not to test remains with the child to decide after he or she is 18.

sections.heading: Methods
sections.text: The author explores her years of unknowing, her efforts to seek support, her mistakes in an extraordinary situation, and the perceived inattention of her daughter's physician to the child's mental health in the absence of testing.

sections.heading: Results/conclusions
sections.text: This account adds to the knowledge about parents who must deal with the unknowns of raising a child with a fifty-fifty chance of having an incurable, genetically inherited adult-onset disease. With revolutionary advances in the field of genetics and the exponential growth of genetic testing, more patients-and parents-may seek out and benefit from the accounts of others dealing with what is sometimes a cloudy crystal ball. This autoethnography also adds to the understanding of physicians about the need for physician support and genetic counseling in such circumstances and augments the rare accounts of CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopathy), a little-known disease that affects only two to five of every 100,000 people.

items.title: Treatment and Patient-Related Concepts in Chronic Scrotal Pain: A Bibliometric and Content Analysis of PubMed Publications.
items.authors: Ortoğlu F, Uysal U.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Chronic scrotal pain can affect daily life, sexual function, and psychological well-being. We examined publication characteristics and dictionary-defined treatment and patient-related terminology in titles and abstracts. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional bibliometric study with exploratory dictionary-based content analysis of PubMed records retrieved using a consolidated search on 31 October 2026, retaining a publication-date cutoff of 10 September 2026 and using OpenAlex citation and affiliation metadata from 31 October 2026. Following the initial assessment, two urologists independently assessed eligibility for a stratified sample of 85 records and concept coding for a stratified sample of 60 publications during revision. Performance of the unchanged dictionary was evaluated against the manual codes for these 60 publications. Seven overlapping categories were assessed in combined titles and abstracts of publications with abstracts. Sensitivity analyses varied eligibility scope and publication types; the original and consolidated datasets were also compared. Results: Of 421 screened journal records, 278 publications from 1979-2026 formed the core corpus. OpenAlex matched 275 publications, with 5216 citations and a corpus h-index of 39. The United States contributed to 131 publications; international collaboration occurred in 23/252 publications with country data (9.1%). Among 232 publications with abstracts, the dictionary matched treatment/management expressions in 84.5%, pain scales/scores in 24.6%, quality of life/function in 18.5%, psychosocial/mental health in 12.9%, sexual symptoms/function in 8.2%, satisfaction/global improvement in 3.9%, and recurrence/durability/reintervention in 11.2%. Treatment/management generated the highest dictionary-match frequency across sensitivity analyses (78.0-82.6%). Internal evaluation showed category-dependent sensitivity, including 22.2% for satisfaction/global improvement and 29.6% for recurrence/durability/reintervention. Conclusions: In this exploratory analysis, the broad treatment/management category generated the most dictionary matches. Unequal category breadth and sensitivity limit direct comparisons; infrequent or absent title/abstract matches do not establish that patient-centered outcomes were unmeasured, inadequately assessed, or unreported in the full text.

items.title: Outcomes of Aesthetic Treatment in Individuals with Body Dysmorphic Disorder in Hospital and Outpatient Settings: A Scoping Review.
items.authors: Vitale NM, Fakhrou A, Licitra N, Sangiorgio A, Schilirò G, Catania C, De Leo BE, Uccelli E, Farruggio G, Frischetto SM, Verduzzo I, Caponnetto P.

sections.text: Background/Objectives: Body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) is characterized by a persistent and intrusive preoccupation with a perceived defect in physical appearance, associated with significant psychosocial impairment. Individuals with BDD frequently seek aesthetic and cosmetic procedures to correct the perceived flaw, yet cosmetic treatment has traditionally been regarded as a relative contraindication in this population, often associated with unsatisfactory outcomes and symptom exacerbation. However, more recent evidence has been heterogeneous, keeping the relationship between BDD and aesthetic treatment outcomes controversial. This scoping review aimed to map the literature of the last decade on the clinical, psychological, and behavioral outcomes of surgical and non-surgical aesthetic procedures performed on individuals with BDD. Methods: This review was conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology for scoping reviews and reported in accordance with the PRISMA extension for Scoping Reviews (PRISMA-ScR). PubMed, Scopus, and EBSCOhost were searched for studies published between 2016 and February 2026 reporting clinical, psychological, or behavioral outcomes of aesthetic procedures (surgical or minimally invasive) in samples with a formal BDD diagnosis or a positive screening result. Study selection and data charting were performed independently by two reviewers. Results: Of 419 records identified, 17 primary studies published between 2016 and 2026 met the inclusion criteria. The included studies varied considerably in design, sample size, BDD assessment methods, aesthetic procedures, outcome measures, and follow-up duration. Several studies reported improvements in BDD-related measures, changes in screening classification, or favorable postoperative satisfaction, whereas others reported less favorable findings. Psychological and behavioral outcomes were assessed inconsistently, and broader psychiatric safety outcomes were rarely investigated. The heterogeneity of the available evidence limited direct comparisons and prevented conclusions regarding treatment effectiveness or psychological safety. Conclusions: The available evidence is limited and highly heterogeneous in study design, populations, procedures, outcome measures, and follow-up duration, and most samples were identified through screening instruments rather than diagnostic interviews. Although several studies reported postoperative improvement and satisfaction in some individuals with BDD symptoms, these findings do not establish the efficacy of aesthetic treatment for BDD and should be interpreted with caution. Future research should jointly examine preoperative BDD severity and treatment expectations as potential predictors of postoperative outcomes.

items.title: Psychobiotics Targeting the Microbiota-Gut-Brain Axis: From Molecular Mechanisms to Clinical Translation.
items.authors: Karaivazoglou K, Aggeletopoulou I, Triantos C.

sections.text: The microbiota-gut-brain axis is a bidirectional communication network linking the intestinal environment with the brain and plays a central role in systemic homeostasis and human health. Disruption of this axis has been repeatedly associated with chronic diseases, including neuropsychiatric disorders. Increasing evidence suggests that selected probiotics and prebiotics, termed psychobiotics, may support mental health through humoral, neural, endocrine, and immune-mediated pathways. This narrative review summarizes animal and human studies to clarify how psychobiotics influence behavioral, cognitive, and emotional processes by modulating the microbiota-gut-brain axis. Preclinical studies consistently show that Lactobacillus and Bifidobacterium strains affect gut-brain signaling through the production of neuroactive compounds and regulation of host genes involved in stress and inflammation. Clinical findings partly support these effects in specific patient populations. Psychobiotics may represent safe, accessible interventions, but stronger validation is needed before routine clinical use and precision psychiatry. Further multidisciplinary research should define mechanisms, responders, and optimal formulations.
